THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with Charlie Barnet by Patricia Willard
Reel 1
April 23, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 847-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S

This is April 23rd, 1978, and we are docked at the Kauna Kai Club at Shelter Island in San Diego, California, and this is the oral history with Charlie Barnet, and Charlie you said you wanted to start when you were born, right?
Well, that would be a good time to start.
Okay. Do the records have it correctly?
October 26, 1913.
That's what I read. And your full name is --
Charles Daly Barnet.
And Daly is D-a-l-y.
D-a-l-y.
Okay. And you were born in New York City?
That's right.
Okay. You said that one of the first things you wanted to do on here was correct a many times repeated legend, right, about --
Well, yes. It's one of those things that keeps cropping up in discographies and some of the people that write the books, about the big band era, and it just
never happened. This is the supposed performance of me on the chimes on Duke Ellington's record of "Ring Them Bells." It just never happened and I have no idea how it ever got started.
But while we were talking about that, while we were setting up the tape recorder, you did mention something that you did on an Ellington record, which was what?

Well, I was pressed into service, more or less in an emergency, because they wanted more Latin sounds, I was pressed into service as a maraca player on one of the small band, Ellington band dates, under Barney Bigard's name, which I believe was -- I think the tune was "Moonlight Fiesta".

And we looked that up in Benny Aslin's (PHONETIC) discography, and we found out that that date was June 16th, 1937, and it was a date with Barney Bigard, Harry Carney, Rex Stewart, Juan Tizol, Duke Ellington, Freddie Guy, Billy Taylor and Sonny Greer.
Right.
And it credits you with maracas. Where was that recording, the session?
That was done in New York at the Master Records, Variety Record Studios, the Irving Mills Recording Company.
I see. And you said it was Irving Mills didn't feel they could spare a horn player to play

Well, he wanted more of a Latin sound than they were getting there, and of course Sonny was the only percussionist there at the moment, and so he suggested that I play the maracas, and that's how I happened to -- I happened to be in the studio.

I see. Back to you and your music. When did you get started? I read in one of the many, many books I've been reading about you that your uncle gave you a saxophone when you were eight years old. Is that correct?

No, it wasn't my uncle. My mother actually bought the horn for me. But it was pretty much in self defense, because I had been very interested in drumming. I had a bunch of her hat boxes all set up and I used to wail away on them, and of course knock a hole in all of them, and I was making a fearful racket with the drums, and I guess they figured that they would be better off with a saxophone than a drum. But they had no idea how horrible a saxophone can sound in the hands of a brand new owner with no lessons.
What kind of a saxophone was it?
It was a C melody.
And were you eight years old when you got it?
Golly, I'd have to think that out. Eight. I think -- that's about right. Maybe nine.
And how long had you been improvising drums?
Well, I used to, like I say, get these hat boxes, and I'd just go in there, in my room, and wail away on them. I guess I was doing that from about seven years of age. And --
Did you listen to a lot of music, or did you just want to make music, or --

Well, we had a phonograph and we also -- you know, we had the radio, the ones with the three dials, where you'd have to be very astute to tune in a station at all. But my mother played the piano, but she was never forced to have to have me as an accompanist on the drums. She escaped that. I'd just wail away by myself. And as most kids do, I mean I probably had a fantasy. I loved the theater, and I used to get a big charge -- I always sat down in the front row, next to the pit drummer. Because most of the theaters in those days, every one of them, had an orchestra, even the neighborhood theaters. And I'd go in there and sit there for two or three shows and watch him. I was completely enthralled with it.
So it was drums from an early age.
Yeah.
Were you able to forget about drums when you got the saxophone?
Well, I was almost forced to, because
I had the saxophone and I didn't have any drums.
Did you ever consider going back to drums when you got older?

No. It was pointed out to me that the drummer had to carry all of this stuff in and set it up and then also break it down and take it away, and also, in those days, strangely enough, apparently the drummer wasn't too well thought of in the orchestras. He was more or less of a glorified band boy in a lot of respects. He had to do a lot of other things of that nature with the orchestra.
Like what, like carry other instruments or --
Well, more or less pass the music out and he really had an awful lot to do. Of course that was before drummers had names.
Can you remember any particular music you heard on the family phonograph that impressed you at an early age?

Well, at that particular age, if we're going to go back as far as that, seven or eight years old, that would be pretty hard to say. I used to hear broadcasts from the nightclubs, and of course they were -- the quality was ridiculous. But I remember hearing a saxophone player at the time, Ross Gorman, and he had an orchestra and he played at a club, I believe it was called the Monte Carlo Club. That was

back in the '20s, then I used to hear Charley Johnson's Orchestra, from Small's Paradise. Which also I was very impressed with. But they used to come on rather late, and I had to kind of sneak, you know, listening to them, because I was supposed to be in bed and asleep.
That was when you were probably how old, that you were listening to the nightclub shows?

Well, I would say this was maybe a little further on, around, oh, 10 or 12. But I remember being very impressed with the Charley Johnson Orchestra. And I remember my mother, she said, "I don't understand what you see in all that."
(Laughter)
What particular part of the music impressed you? What did you like?

Well, I thought it was exciting, I mean, and interesting, and inventive. I mean it was different, let's put it that way. Of course then it was closely after that that I, through phonograph records, I became aware of the Ellington Orchestra. And that was really an extension of my interest in the Charley Johnson Orchestra, because the soloists in the Ellington Band, I mean, were so distinct, and they had such a distinct quality, that to me it was most interesting.
Did Charley Johnson's band -- I'm not -- I don't know about it, so, did it have interesting soloists also?

Well, they -- let's put it this way, it was a swinging band for that era. They had a drummer, I can't remember his last name, his name was George something, he was just excellent. And let's see, I don't know if they were in the band at that time, but at one time the trumpet players were Bill Coleman and Frank Newton. And it was, oh, I guess they had -- well, it was just like two trumpets and a trombone and three saxophones and four rhythm. It wasn't, you know, one of those huge bands. But none of the bands were at that time, except possibly Paul Whiteman.
And did he interest you?

Well, yeah, I used to go see him when he would play a theater or something like that, because I was too young to go into clubs. And I was impressed with Paul Whiteman. He was something to watch himself. I mean he was definitely the leader of the band, there was no question about that, and of course the band was so huge that it was -- you know, for that time, that alone was something that you just had to go see and hear.
So when did you -- you first heard Ellington, it would have been when he started the broadcast from --
No, I became aware of Ellington through records. I got ahold of some records. I can't remember who or where or when, but it was very early. And it sounded

different than anything that I'd ever heard, and I liked it. And I more or less kept buying them, you know, right on through the process where he went from the smaller band into the five brass and the four saxophone. I remember one time everybody on the street -- this was probably a little later -- they said, "Tommy Dorsey's playing with Duke Ellington." And I said, "You're kidding, he can't be." And what had happened, of course, Juan Tizol was the one, and Juan was very light in color and he wore the glasses, and the false rumor got out, you know, that Tommy Dorsey was playing trombone with Duke Ellington.
But his trombone didn't slide anymore, right?
No.
(Laughter)
That's funny. Do you remember at what age you decided that you wanted to be a musician?
Well, I think I always wanted to be. It was --
Back to the hatbox days?

Yeah, back to the hatbox days. And while I wasn't encouraged about it, I wasn't stomped on about it. I mean, nobody said, "Don't you dare touch that horn again," or anything like that. And then I didn't, like, go against the complete wishes of my family, as some people would
have you believe.
I have read somewhere that your family wanted you to be an attorney. Is that right?

Well, they probably would have liked that, but I know my mother -- I asked her one time, I said, "Now, I see you, you're here opening nights and you're around and everything like that. Now, if I'd have been a lawyer, you couldn't have done that." No, I think she was very happy with it, the way it turned out, after all.

I read that you left school when you were 16 to lead a band. I read two different versions. I read one that you began your musical career by leading a band on an ocean liner, and then I read in another source that you played in bands on ocean liners and later had your own band. Which is right?

Well, actually the first band I had was quite a large band for that particular time, and it also happened to have been a non-union band. There was a restaurant on Broadway, upstairs, a Chinese-American restaurant, at the corner of 50th, where -- yes, 50th Street and Broadway, and they had gotten into some kind of a beef with the union, and somehow or other I got a band together and I called myself Fred Black.
(Laughter)
And we had -- oh, let's see, it was the

usual combination for those days, like two trumpets, trombone, three saxophones and the rhythm section, and I think we worked all of four days before they finally made peace with the union, and they threw us out then.
Was that your first band?
Yeah.
Oh.
And it was after that in that year -- that was in 1929 -- that I got the job as the ship's orchestra on the S. S. Republic.
Which went where?
It went from New York to Bremerhaven. And -- Germany and back.
So that would have-- you were 16, right?
Yeah. That was the summertime of '29.
And it was --
It was after the Fred Black episode.
Were you a member of the union at 16?
I wasn't at the time I was Fred Black.
I see. But you were protecting your good name for the time that you would be a union musician or what? Why did you use a different name?
I don't know. I just decided that would be a good name for some reason or other. I didn't really
But it was just as well.

The union was terribly weak at that time, anyway. It wasn't really much chance of getting in much trouble, because there wasn't anybody in town that was getting paid union scale, except maybe some studio musicians, and even that the rates were so low, like you'd go into a recording studio and for 20 bucks you'd be expected to do as many sides as you could put out.
Uh-huh.
So there really wasn't any -- that didn't come into account. But I did join the union later, naturally.
You -- what had you done -- did you have private lessons -- your first professional job was as a band leader. What did you do before you were a band leader? Did you just -- did you play with anybody?

Well, I got jobs around in some of the -- oh, I worked at a Chinese-American restaurant on 23rd Street, while I was still going to school, called the Golden Pheasant. And what I'd do is I'd -- I was going to a school called Berkeley-Irving on West 83rd Street, and I'd come in and I'd answer the opening roll call, and then because I'd been up so late the night before, I was sleepy, I'd go down in the basement, they had a place there, where I'd crawl in and go to sleep, and

then I would go out of there and go down and play the noon session and come back and answer the roll call out at the end of the school day. And then I'd go back and play the dinner session and then the late session, and school was definitely getting in the way.
(Laughter)
How long did you do that before you just gave up on school?

Well, I lasted through about one year of that. Of course I wasn't working all the time. But you asked me where I had worked. Well, that was one. I also did a lot of club jobs around New York. You know, what they called later one nighters.
Casuals?
Or in California now they call them casuals. But they were some pretty weird places, some pretty weird money, you know, like $6.00 a night or something like that.
Did you work with any interesting musicians on any of those?

Well, you see, at that time in New York there were places where the musicians hung out, and it wasn't at the union. At 46th Street and Broadway, there was the Gaiety Theater Building there. There was also the Gaiety, the billiard room, down in the basement. Now, all the guys hung out on 46th Street. However, this was the lowest step

in the echelon, because on 48th Street and Broadway, this was where all of the guys that were really with it, that's where they hung out, and you had to graduate from 46th Street to 48th Street. You weren't just automatically accepted. You had to do something to -- otherwise -- for example, the jobs you got out of 46th Street didn't pay nearly as much as the ones that you got out of 48th Street. And a cop used to come along and chase everybody on both corners. But the minute he was gone, they'd all be right back there. It was kind of an interesting time, because across Times Square, all of the actors were out in front of the Palace Theater, and the musicians, you know, on these two corners, it was quite a scene.

And then the big thing was at night. These were, oh, when great stories had told of how they had -- the heroic events that they had done musically, in front of the Lido Sandwich Shop, on 50th Street and Broadway. Now, between -- that's right between Broadway and 7th. The block is about 100 feet long at that place, and there was a hotel upstairs called the Glencourt Hotel, which a lot of musicians lived in. But at night, you know, after about 2:00 o'clock in the morning, oh, guys like Louis Garsha (PHONETIC) and Bill Moore, they'd all gather there after they'd done their gigs, and a lot of tall tales were told. But if you got up in that bunch, that was -- you were really making it then.
So you got -- it was from 46th to
48th to 50th.
To 50th, yeah.
(Laughter)
What was at 48th, besides -- I mean was there any establishment or just a corner?
No, it was just a corner.
Not like a theater or a restaurant or a hotel.

No, just a place where -- well, there was a bunch of restaurants around the corner, off of Broadway there, and people could get coffee and doughnuts and things like that. But I rather imagine it just happened by itself.
Was the Gaiety Delicatessen there then, or did that come later? I mean at 46th.

No, I don't remember. All I remember is the Gaiety Theater Building, which was full of these agents and then the poolroom down below. Of course the theater was there, but these agents were something else. There was Louis' Booking Office and above all people, Harry Moss -- Mal Hallett and Harry Moss had a booking office up there. But that was the best one in the building. Of course Harry Moss later went on and he was with MCA and became really a number one booking agent. But Harry had a lot of the school dates, and Louis' Booking Office was booking bands on all these ships and there was another one there called Rocco's Booking
Office, and he was selling little bands to all the Catskill Mountains hotels and the summer jobs and things like that. A real crummy setup.
(Laughter)
And that's where you got the booking on the ship, is that right?

I have the contract home, incidentally. Would you believe that we got $150.00 a month for the whole band, which of course included our room, you know, stateroom on the ship, and food. But that was it.
How long was the crossing?
Well, it was for round -- that's for a month -- in the course of the month we would make two trips, you know, round trips.
I see. And so that was your beginning in the professional music business.

Yeah. I later played in another band on the Pennland (PHONETIC) -- the Republic was the United States Line, and the Pennland was the Red Star Line, and that orchestra was under the direction of Buzz Meredith, who happened to be Burgess Meredith's brother.
Oh.
And we made a couple of trips. I think we were called the Ohio State something or other.
What did he play?
He played drums when he was sober enough to find the sticks.
So what -- after you left the -- your first ship date, right - the Meredith, right -- I mean, no, the --
The Republic?
The Republic, yeah. Where did you go from there?

Well, I think it was shortly after that that I became involved with Frank Winegard (PHONETIC), who had a band called Frank Winegard and His Pennsylvanians. And Frank had played at Young's Restaurant, which is another Chinese-American restaurant. There was a lot of those around and most of them used bands in those days, and they were all three sessions. You played noon, and then you played dinner and you played you know, supper. They were tough jobs. They didn't pay well and it was hard work. But Frank had played there and he had gotten a little air time, and he got a band together, and we played a place called the Village Barn. And we were there quite a long time. Of course we did some other things, some one nighters, and short jobs around, but that was the longest stint with him.
I'll tell you something funny about that, if you -- I was at that time not exactly the greatest reader in the world. My formal musical education had -- I had studied

piano for a couple of years. I knew the notes and everything, and I took some saxophone lessons from one of the Brown Brothers. There used to be a saxophone band called The Six Brown Brothers, and I had taken lessons from one of them.
Which one?

Harry Voltaire (PHONETIC). There was nobody by the name of Brown in the whole band. It was just a bunch of guys that called themselves that. A fellow by the name of Harry Voltaire. And he gave me one lesson. I came back the next day and played him the whole score from "Wildflower", and instead of getting a pat on the head he read the riot act to me. Oh, he really laid me out for doing that. And I understand why now, because I was blessed with a good ear and he didn't want me to use the ear. He wanted me to learn to read properly. Well, you see, I hadn't at this time. And I worked for a whole year with Frank Weingard, and the rest of the band was so bad -- I don't mean that I was that much better -- but the band was so bad that by the time they got done hassling -- they only used stock orchestrations and a few, maybe a half a dozen, special arrangements, as they were called, which they weren't, by the time they got done hassling their parts out I already had a part made up. Now, I must point out there was only three saxophones, so it wasn't very difficult to make up a part out of your head. And I never got out a part the whole time I was with the band. I told Frank I had them all memorized. And he used to tell

people that. He'd say, "My, look at this kid here. He's got all the parts memorized." Well, this was fine, except we got -- we were going to make a record date, and we got in the studio there and we had this recording guy there by the name of Schubert (PHONETIC). I don't remember his first name, but he was one of those fellows that if you tapped an ashtray, he'd say, "That's a B." And we started, and he said, "Stop the band." He said, "Who is playing a G in the second and third beats of the fourth bar?" No answer, you know, so he came out in the studio and he said, "All right, let me hear the saxophones play it." Well, we started and he said, "Hold it." He said, "This man can't read," pointing at me. Because I was making up -- I had a part I had made up and that wasn't on the music. What I had there, I had changed the harmony, I guess. And of course Frank was completely -- oh, he was furious. He fired me. And then, about a day later -- oh, less than a day later, he got to thinking about it, and he said, "My goodness, if you were good enough to fool me for a whole year, if you'll promise to study and get up on your reading," he said, "You can stay in the band."
(Laughter)
I can imagine, you know, how embarrassing this must have been to him.
So you then began to study to learn how to read.
Well, I knew how to read. I just didn't -- I hadn't been putting it in practice. Naturally, like anything else, you have to -- so I started playing the parts. I still think mine were better.
They probably were. So you went back with Winegar then.

Yes. We finished out that engagement. Then Frank really didn't go anyplace from there. He was a very nice man. One of the things -- he had had infantile paralysis, and he had one leg that was, you know, very badly deformed, small, and he wore a metal brace there. And he used to horrify us. He'd yell up to the trombone player, "Throw me the oil, " and then he'd roll up his leg and squirt the trombone oil on the brace, and -- I don't know.
At what point did you begin playing tenor saxophone?
I was playing tenor saxophone in Winegar's band.
When did you start?
Well, I'd changed to -- first I got an alto -- you mean after the C melody?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
First I got an alto, and I fiddled around with that, and then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and I said, "Oh, I've got to play the tenor," and so I got myself a tenor.

And I stayed with the tenor for quite a number of years after that. In fact I used the tenor right on up, oh, until recent years, when I decided that I'd better just confine myself to alto and soprano.
When did you start playing soprano?

Believe it or not, I played the soprano in a school band, because they needed one. They had enough of the others, and although I didn't -- I always liked it, but I didn't have one, and at the time it wasn't too well thought of as an instrument, and those old sopranos, believe it or not, they were terribly treacherous. I mean the intonation was almost -- to achieve even a fair average of intonation was almost impossible.
That was the [Burkley Irving] band that you played in?
No, that was a band that -- at Riverdale, Riverdale Country School that I went to.
That was before you went to Burkley Irving, is that right?

Well, I went to Burkley Irving twice. I went to -- this was between Burkley Irving things. I went to Burkley Irving once, I was quite young, and then I went to Riverdale Country School, and I wasn't exactly popular with the headmaster there because he -- they had a very pretty waitress there that used to wait on tables and I was caught in her room with a flask of gin.
At what age?
(Laughter)
And then you left Riverdale?

Yes. I wasn't exactly expelled, but as they say, he who runs away lives to fly another day. And then I went to school for half a year out in New Trier High School, in Chicago. Not really Chicago, it was Indian Hill, which was right next to Winnetka.
What was the name of the school again?
New Trier.
How do you spell that?
Well, capital N-e-w, capital T-r-i-e-r. It's still there. It's quite a famous old high school.
And you went there how long?

I went there up until the middle of the year, when I went home for Christmas. My family -- we had lost my grandfather, who was the man in the family, and I was -- my aunt and uncle lived out there, so I went out there to go to school, and I never went back. That's when I ran away.
(Laughter)
Although I loved them dearly. They were wonderful people and I guess I was pretty happy there.
It was school you weren't happy with, is that right?

No, on the contrary. I mean I was very happy with the school, but I liked New York. This was at the time just a little bit too rural for my tastes. Because It was quite rural at that time. Now I guess it's all built in like everything else is.
So you went to -- the last school you went to was the New Trier School, not Burkley Irving.
No, I went to Burkley Irving after New Trier.
Oh, I see.
You see, I came -- let's get this -- yeah -- no, no. We've got it -- we've got Blair Academy in there someplace.
All right. That's I think the only school name I've read in any of the material about you, is Blair Academy.
Well, that was in 1926. I think I went to Blair after the New Trier -- no, I was at Blair before New Trier. That's right.
And Riverdale before Blair?
Oh, Riverdale was -- oh, yes, definitely. It would go in this order. Burkley Irving, Riverdale, then Blair, then New Trier, and then back to Burkley.
I see. Okay. And did anyplace besides Riverdale have a school band?
Well, all of them had bands.
Did you play in all of them?
I didn't play in the New Trier band. But I played in the band -- I played tuba in the Blair band.
Oh. And soprano at Riverdale.
At Riverdale.
And what did you play at Burkley Irving?
Well, they didn't have a band.
Oh.
They --
You wouldn't have had time anyway, if you were --
No, I was already -- the second time -- I was much too young to play in any band the first time in Burkley and the second time I was already making it out in the real thing.
I see. So your first experience with soprano was at Riverdale.
Yeah, around in 1922.
And then by the time you were 16 you had a tenor? Is that right?
Yes. Yes.
And --
See, I never owned a soprano until Billy May brought an arrangement in back in 1939 or '40, with
a soprano part, and I said, "I haven't got a soprano, Billy." And he said, "Well, go buy one, the part's here." And I did.
And you hadn't played on in all those years?

No. Like I say, they didn't have a very good reputation amongs -- now, my God, everybody's playing them. But even when I started playing it there, I -- besides Johnny Hodges and Sidney Bechet, that's about all there was.
Uh-huh. In addition to your Atlantic crossings, John Chilton mentions that you also crossed the Mediterranean and cruised to South America. Is that right?

Well, I was on a Mediterranean cruise in 1926 with my parents, at the conclusion of which we visited Paris and London, but I did play on a Caribbean cruise on the old Mauritania, the old four stacker.
Was that the only one towards South America?
Yes.
I see. Okay. And Leonard Feather mentions in his encyclopedia that you crossed the ocean 22 times, later went to the South Seas and Latin America. Is that a good count?
Well, I don't know. I'm glad it's an even number, because I couldn't have gotten back where I was.
(Laughter)
That speaks for its accuracy, then.

I think that's a little exagerarrated, because, let's see, there's two, four -- I'm thinking of the Republic and the Pennland. Of course I did travel with my parents quite a bit on some of these trips.
But did you play?
No, not --
I see. Because the implication is that -- he doesn't actually say so, though, but the implication is that you were playing all those trips.
Well, this is another one of those things, over a period of time that becomes -- like you say, it doesn't say so, but it winds up meaning that.
Uh-huh. Well, that's what we want to clear up if we can. Let's get your parents' names. They were what?
My father was Willard Barnet.
Oh, good name.
And my mother was Charlene Daley, before she was a Barnet.
And your grandfather?
My grandfather was Charles Frederick Daley. My grandmother was Edith Clarke Daley.
Okay. Those were your maternal grandparents. Do you know your paternal grandparents' names?
No, I don't.
And it was your maternal grandfather who was connected with the railroad, is that right?

Yes. He started out in life as a telegraph operator, in I believe it was Lima, Ohio, and he went on up the ladder there and finally became executive first vice president of the Grand Central -- I mean the New York Central Railroad. And at the time, World War I, when the government took the railroad over, he was so upset with the way they were handling things that he resigned, and he went in with W. C. Durant, who was an automobile manufacturer. He had -- well, they made the Durant, they made the Locomobile, they made the Star and the Flint, and the -- during that time he also became President of the Liberty National Bank. How he was able to do all that I don't know. I also discovered in some of the papers that were passed on down to me that he was on the Board of Directors of some 45 different companies, which completely amazes me. He was a wonderful man. I have nothing but fond memories of him, because he took the -- my father was divorced when I was two years old and I have no recollection of him at all. I never met him. He died in -- oh, shortly after I opened in the Paramount Hotel, which was in November of '32, and he had been remarried and I don't know, he -- well, I just never heard from him, I never saw him. I've got pictures of him, but -- but my grandfather stepped
into this void and was more or less of a father to me.
Did he encourage your music?

Well, like I said before, he didn't exactly encourage it, but he didn't really discourage it. I remember the first time they caught me smoking, and oh, I was going to Blair Academy, I think. I was 15 then. And they said -- they had a smoking room there. All the kids had been getting caught smoking, you know, and finally the headmaster said, "I'm going to establish a smoking room and those who can get permission from their parents will be allowed to use it." So everybody else wrote, and I called up my mother and I said, "Look, you don't want me to be caught out behind the gymnasium smoking a cigarette, because I'm going to do it. Why don't you wire permission for me to smoke" which she did, and here I am, all the seniors and everything there, they hadn't got their permission, I'm the only one in the smoking room. I'm sitting in there, lighting it up. But my grandfather, I'll never forget, he said, "If you're going to smoke," this was when I got home, he said, "Now, if you're going to smoke," he said, "I want you to smoke a good cigarette," and he gave me a cigarette case and a package of Camels.
And how long did you smoke Camels?
I smoked them for years.
And now you're using filters, right?
Oh, I'm down to the lowest tar that you can find, the lowest -- you hear so much it scares you to
death, but I can't quite. I've tried it -- I quit for five months twice, but something happens and all of a sudden you light one up and you're gone again.
Camels are rough, though.

Oh, they were strong. After you smoke these filters and somebody comes up with one of those -- well, they don't make those anymore, I don't think, the old type Camels. You'd inhale that and the whole room would start spinning, you know.
I remember how strong they were. According to the Chilton book, you -- what is this Rumsey Academy?
Oh, that was very early. I went there one year. That was up in Connecticut. That was sometime -- I would say that was between Burkley Irving and Riverdale.
So that you would have been maybe 11 or 12 or something, maybe 11.
It says here you played in the school band, which you left for almost a year, to play for almost a year with Frank Weingard. But that's not right.
No, that's not right, because I was very young when I went to Rumsey Hall and they didn't have a band, although I did have a saxophone, I remember that.
It was Rumsey Hall, not Rumsey Academy?
No, Rumsey Hall.
Okay. Then after Frank Weinagar Weingard, it says here you left New York with Beasley Smith. Is that right, was that next?

Well, more or less. There was probably a little -- let's see, I rehearsed and played a few things with, oh, a band by the name of Houston Ray and Will Osborne, and but then I joined Beasley. Beasley was a travelling band. He was out of Nashville, Tennessee, and I joined his band and we toured around all over New England and Pennsylvania and parts of the south. Not the deep south. Virginia and North Carolina and Tennessee.
How big was the Beasley Smith band?

It was the same thing there. We had the three brass, two trumpets, trombone and three saxophones, and of course Beasley was the piano player, and the guitar, bass and drums. That was the standard instrumentation in those days.
And so that would have been about what year?

Well, let's see, that would be after Frank Weinagar Weingard, and I guess that would be around 1930, maybe into '31. And following -- well, we broke up. Beasley started to lose his eyesight and he had to disband the band. Fortunately he didn't lose it. They were able to rectify it. But -- and

that's when I decided to investigate the south. I'd heard so much about all these guys coming out of there, you know, Teagarden and Louis Armstrong out of New Orleans, and so I went -- I got -- I had a friend of mine, a trumpet player who had played in that band that was on the S. S. Pennland, a fellow by the name of Gordon Tulley, and he was working with Flem Ferguson and the Washington-Erie Hotel in Shreveport, Louisiana, and he got me on the band there, and well, that was a delightful job. We -- for our work at the hotel we got our room, $10.50 a week allowance for food in the coffee shop, and no money. The only way we got any cash at all was, see, we only played a noon session and a dinner session, and the only way we got any money at all was on Saturday night we'd play at the country club and we'd get seven bucks or something like that, or if you could pick up some other place to play, individually, you know, not as a band, you might pick up another night in some little joint there for four or five bucks, and that was the only way we got any money.
Was that a fairly big hotel?
Oh, yes. It's -- it was the biggest hotel in town. In fact it was a combination of two hotels. They were connected.
Was that a common practice for big hotels to pay so little, I mean to pay nothing?
Well, you have to remember this was at

the height of the depression, and to have a band at all was a complete luxury, and I can't speak for -- I've heard of some funny stories about some of the deals these bands had. This to me is the worst deal I've heard of. However, you want to know something? I can't remember a happier time in my life than those days at the Washington-Erie.
Why, were you playing great music, or just having a good time, or --

Well, it was a great bunch of guys and we -- let's see, Harry James was in that band for awhile. And oh, Tommy Goslin and Truitte Jones and Curtis Hurt and, oh, the arranger -- oh, he later arranged a lot for the Bob Crosby band -- oh, a saxophone player. I can't think of his name. He's been an important arranger. I'll think of it. But he was in the band, he was writing arrangements for it, and it was quite a pleasant time. Of course that came to an end and I went to work in -- over in the east Texas oil fields, in what they called a keg house, and -- Kilgore, Texas. It was a boom town, an oil boom town. If you've never been in one you have no idea. It's -- the people there, the streets were mud. In the keg house you kicked the band off at 8:00 o'clock and you didn't quit playing until 3:00 o'clock in the morning. And the booze was about two hours old. They had nothing but sugar whiskey and they had it in these fruit jars, and everybody was walking around with a mark on the bridge of their nose

from drinking out of the fruit jars. And there was a continuous fight going on there all the time. A real hard, rough job, and everything was very expensive. When it would rain the streets were so bad there was guys that made a living, they'd charge you fifty bucks to carry you across the street, because the mud got so deep, that east Texas red clay.
Yeah, I know about that, but --
Yeah, I got my head busted with a bottle down there, wound up in the pokey, and got out of there and got out of town.
Wow. How long were you there altogether?
I must have been there about a month.
And you went there from Shreveport?
Yeah.
How long were you in Shreveport?
Well, I was at Shreveport a couple of times. This was in between. This was after the first time. I went back to New York after that.
From Texas?
From Texas, yeah. After you get your head busted in, I said, maybe I'd better go back to New York.
More civilized, yeah. So --
But the second time we went to Shreveport, to the hotel there, I took Jack Purvis and a trumpet player by the name of Harley Booth, and a guitar player by the name

of Scoop Thompson, and we joined Flem's band and we used to play up in the roof garden there in the summertime, and Jack Purvis is a -- I don't know if you've ever heard of him -- he was a fantastic musician, a fantastic trumpet player. He could do everything that Louis Armstrong could do in those days. He had a tremendous range for those days. He had himself a G or an A anytime he wanted it. And well, the Louisiana Symphony came to town, and Jack somehow got himself into a deal there where he was going to play the Carnival of Venice with the symphony, and he was rehearsing with them. That and something else he was going to play. And Jack was pretty crazy. For no reason whatsoever he says, "Come on, let's go to California." And I said, "Well, you've got to do that thing with the symphony." He said, "Oh, the hell with it." So we got in the car and we left, and we got out as far as El Paso, and it seems that Jack had been there before, and he had been smuggling guns across the border in his previous time there, and the people that were in power at the time he was smuggling were now out of power, and we beat a hasty retreat. We got split up. And I went on to the Coast. I didn't see him at all until one night, I walked into the old Cotton Club out in Culver City. I had no idea what had happened to him. And I heard this trumpet, and I looked up at the bandstand, and here's Purvis up there, he's got his face stained and he's playing trumpet with Les Heidt's orchestra.
(Laughter)
Now, I said, "What are you doing?" He said, "Sshh, don't tell anybody who I am. They're after me."
(Laughter)
I said, "Who's after you?" He said, "The government." I think he was probably right. I didn't believe him at the time, but he did wind up spending his last days in jail.
For the gun smuggling?

I don't know what for. He had, oh, like seven or eight wives with no divorces, and he used to steal the Western Union boys' bicycles, and he was a thoroughly crazy man, but very talented. Well, I'll give you an example. When we left to go from New York down to Shreveport, Jack was playing first trumpet with Waring's Pennsylvanians, which of course was a very collegiate outfit, and he had been added to the band because Waring was playing at the Roxy Theater, and they had expanded the orchestra to -- you see the scene, in the pit, they were playing the Overture of 1812, which starts out with the trumpet. And now the little pin spot picks Waring up, he comes out of the wings, walks around and goes tip tip, and gives the down beat, and the pin spot comes on the trumpet player, which is Purvis. Now, Jack had a pride and joy of his, which was a little waxed moustache, which he kept cut, you know, and everything. And Waring, it upset him, Waring. Waring said, "Look, Jack," he said, "this is a

college band, Waring's Pennsylvanians. You look like a French count or something. Now please take that off." So Jack cut it off, but he also cut every hair on his head off, he shaved his head. So the next show, here comes Waring out in the spotlight and goes bing, bing, and the spotlight comes on Jack, and there he is, bald headed, no moustache, and Waring, said, "Out." And that's how come we happened to go down south.
(Laughter)
Well, it sounds like it wasn't dull at all with him, right? In addition to playing Shreveport, it says here that he was with you in Kilgore, is that right?
No, he was never in Kilgore with me.
Oh, well --
That was before he had been -- it was the second trip to Shreveport that he --
You went to Shreveport then to Kilgore, then back to New York, then back to Shreveport.
Yeah.
And then to the west coast.
Yeah.
Well, they have it in a different order here. And they have a lot of material about Jack Purvis in the Chilton book, but none of your stories.
Oh, he was something.
Yeah, it mentions his having been in
prison in --

Jack later played in my band at the -- when we left the -- well, he joined me at the Paramount Hotel. He wasn't with me when I opened there, but before we closed he was with us. Then we went to -- oh, up in Albany, to the New Kenmore Hotel. He was on that job with the band. That's the last I ever saw of him.
You went from Shreveport, then, to the West Coast.
Yeah.
To Texas with him and then to the West Coast.
Yeah.
And on the West Coast, according to Chilton, you were free lancing, and then you moved back to New York. With whom on the West Coast?

Well, actually, this saxophone player, a guy by the name of Ralph Spangler, he was there with me, and we kind of joined up with another guy by the name of Tim Lanfier, who was also a saxophone player, and we had like a saxophone section. And I can't tell you the names of anybody we played with there because we were never with anybody that long, because we were totally unruly and we would join the band as a section and we would leave as a section. If anybody said boo to one of us all three of us would leave. And we

played around with, oh, just the local bands there. I couldn't tell you the name of one of them, at that time in California. I think about the only bands that anybody had ever heard of were the Burnett Band, Earl Burnett, and he was at the Biltmore, and then there was the Gus Arnheim Orchestra. Then maybe up in San Francisco there was a band up there. I can't think of his name at the moment, but Phil Harris, he didn't even -- he was still the Loughner Lofner Harris Orchestra. Phil played drums and sat down. In fact nobody stood up. They just -- he was just in the front row with the drums.
Where were they working?
I -- I can't remember the name of the place. It was some ballroom. I can see it. It was down there on Pershing Square. It was up on the second floor.
The Biltmore?

No, no. It was only a two story building. It was on the same square as the Biltmore, but I can't remember the name of the ballroom. I don't know if it's still there or not. I'm sure it isn't as a ballroom, but --
Don't have too many of those anymore. You said you mentioned you went to Sebastian's Cotton Club while you were out here. Who was in Les Hite's Heidt's band then?
Lionel Hampton. Marshall Royal. Let's see, Lawrence Brown, and of course Louis Armstrong came in there, you know, and did all the recording with that
band.
Uh-huh.

But Lionel -- with every band that came in there, even when Earl Hines came in there later, they made Earl leave his drummer out, and Lionel had to -- Frank Sebastian said, 'No, there's only one guy plays drums in this place, and that's Lionel.'
Wow.
Rather upsetting, you know, if you walked in with Gene Krupa or somebody in your band, and you'd say, 'Wait a minute, we've got our own drummer.'
Well, they were like the house band at --

Yeah. They had had these big shows there. Like Timmy Rogers, I remember him, he was in the show there, and they didn't have any -- they didn't go in for any names, but they had the chorus line and oh, they had singers and comedians, and it was quite a colorful place. Of course the gambling room was upstairs.
I never knew about that.

Oh, yeah. In California in those days there was a lot of unofficial gambling went on. You know, quite openly. And that was the place where Pops and Vic Burton got arrested the first time they ever heard of marijuana in California. They had them on the deal, and they

didn't know what to do about it, because there wasn't any real law in the book covering the thing. So what would happen was they would -- they'd take them to work and let them work, and at the end of the night they'd take them back to jail, while they figured out what they were going to do about it.
I read some account of that where it was suggested that Pops was set up for the arrest. By whom, I don't know, a rival ballroom operator or something.

Well, I'm quite sure that things like that have gone on and still do go on. And it's quite possible that this might have happened. But the funny part was they set him up but they didn't have any law to -- that brought about the first legislation for marijuana in the State of California.
I didn't know that.
It wasn't even mentioned in the narcotic laws, you know.
The law makers didn't know we had any.
No, they weren't aware of it.
That's interesting. Did you ever go to the Apex Club?
Oh, yeah. The Dunbar Hotel?
Yeah.
Sure. The Apex, that was on one side
and the Alhambra was on the other side of -- both ends of the hotel.
Alabam, wasn't it?
Alabam, yeah. Yeah.
Who was working there then?

Oh, golly, I don't know. I remember there was a drummer by the name of Freddie Green, who did everything that Lionel did, you know. I think he'd been watching him pretty closely, and throwing the sticks around, and I remember he was in one of the bands. But I couldn't tell you the name of the bands. We used to get together with a lot of the musicians and have jam sessions, particularly in the -- there was a place there, I think it was called Green's, it was a little restaurant, a little nothing restaurant, you know, and they had a piano there and we'd get in there and we'd have jam sessions. I remember one time we had a jam session in a church in Watts. There was a white saxophone player by the name of Bill Covey, and Lionel Hampton and let's see, there was me and then there was Purvis, and it seems to me that what's his -- there was a saxophone player by the name of Bumps --
Bumps Meyers?
Bumps Meyers, yeah. I think he was there.
Yeah. He was very active in L.A.
Yeah. Oh, and Eddie Beale.
Good old Eddie Beale.
Yeah. And we had this wonderful session going on in this church and then daylight, we came out of there it was broad daylight.
Wow. Were there a lot of -- there were a lot of sessions going on, right? I mean musicians did get together and play a lot, or was it hard to find a place to play?
Oh, sure. Like I played -- a white drummer by the name of Bob Forrest and I played with Eckles Dixie Rhythm Kings. We had a trumpet player by the name of Buck Clayton, I mean at the time.

You know, there's been so little recorded, written down, about the music going on in Los Angeles in those days. I mean nobody documented it, and I'm very interested in knowing about it, because I wasn't old enough to get out and hear it yet. But I'm finding out that there was an awful lot of interesting musical activity happening.

Well, there was, but there weren't a lot of people involved. They were more or less the same group. Like if you got by whoever Les Hite had, you had pretty well picked the capable players. There wasn't much left. Well, C. L. Burke, he was the one who played the

Hawaiian guitar, and he was the guitar player in that band. But -- the one that made some records with Pops. But if you went by that group the next step down was a big step. But this Eckles, he used to wear a white suit, and he wore a white hat, something like the one I've got on here. And he was a trumpet player too. And he used to play -- do you know what a gloria trumpet it? That's a straight trumpet, just like the one they call the horses out with, only it had valves. And Buck Clayton was in the band. He was the other trumpet player. And Bob Forrest and I played some one nighters around L.A. with the band. This was back in '29, '30, or -- we may have been the first mixed band, I don't know.
Gee. That was -- yeah. There wasn't any mixing on bandstands, right?

Oh, no. Not in public. There was plenty of it went on in sessions. I mean all the guys used to get together and not only in L.A., but in New York and Chicago and every other place. There'd always be a session going someplace. Particularly I remember up in -- this was a little later on, a couple of years later, but we always used to go up to the Alexander Bar and Grill, on the corner of 7th Avenue and 126th Street, up in Harlem, and they had a back room there. That's the first place I ever met Billie Holiday. She was --

At the end of Reel 1 you were just about to tell me about a place in -- or were you just starting to tell me -- in Harlem.

The cops would come in and raid the place and we'd go out on the street, and I guess the guy that owned the place had the fix in, and he would give us the sign, the minute the cops were gone, and we'd come right back in and start right in again.
(Laughter)
Do you remember what guys from the Ellington band that you would run into in there?

trombone player there, his name escapes me, that played with Fletcher too. He used to be there. And I think Bill Coleman would drop in now and then. Oh, it actually depended who was in town. Were there many white musicians who jammed in Harlem?

No. The group was, I would say, it might be -- I've been there when I was the only white guy, and I've been there when it was, you know, three or four more white guys there. There wasn't any -- you know, just whoever was there. And we all had a ball, we really did.
I remember Benny Goodman used to go and listen, but he never sat in.
Well, I never saw Benny there, but --
I don't mean at that particular place, but I mean uptown at sessions, I've heard musicians say that Benny Goodman used to go and listen but he never played.
Now that you mention it, having been one of those that did go around to a lot of those places, I

don't ever recall seeing Benny play anyplace. Of course they had a wonderful band down at Dickie Weish1 place, down there in the basement. It was a rhythm section, a real swinging rhythm section, and Kenny Rosewall, I think his name was, Kenny something. And the front line were three kazoos, which were attached -- those old time radio loud speakers with the horn, you know?
Uh-huh.
And they had arrangements, and boy, this thing just swung like mad.
Amplified kazoo.
Yeah. A la Rudy Vallee.
Did you get to know Billie, Billie Holiday, there, or you just heard her there?

Oh, well, I met her there, but I didn't really get to know her until later, later on. But in fact she was the one that reminded me of it. She said, "You know, the first time I saw you," and she recalled it, and I said, "Oh, my goodness. That's right, that was you."
In the bobby socks, right?
Yeah.
She -- you've read, "Lady Sings the Blues?"
Oh, yeah.
Was that the way it happened, in the
Well, I don't know. I mean something happened there. Of course -- let's put it this way. Roughly that is about the way it happened, but when you smooth it out it isn't exactly that way.
You -- I know this is not like in chronological order, but since you've mentioned Billie Holiday, do you want to tell us how it happened?
I really don't remember. I don't remember it happening in the way it was described in 'Lady Sings the Blues.'
Uh-huh.
I know there was a scene there, and exactly what happened, it's gone. But to me, I don't think the way it was put in the book is exactly the way it happened.
Well, sometimes those things, as told to, get twisted around a little bit.
Yeah, because something like that had happened with Hazel Scott, too.
What happened with Hazel Scott?
Well, they fired her.
For what, for sitting at a table with you, or -- which is what Billie says happened.
Yeah. And that's why I've often wondered if somebody didn't get the two stories mixed up. Now, I can't tell you which way or who or what, but those things did
happen. There was definitely a no-no, I mean to be overly friendly with a black person at that time.
Even on 52nd Street, or especially on 52nd Street, or how --

Well, now, it depended on the bosses. I mean, you'd get right down to it. I mean like Joe Helblock, next door at the Onyx Club, was very liberally minded. There wasn't any problem there. I didn't happen to have one.
Oh. But if you had wanted to could you have, do you think, or do you know?
I don't know. I really don't. I think that I could have gotten away with it. Because I think those guys that ran that place, I mean if you were doing business

This was before they had the big bands. This was the time like when the Louis Prima band was playing in there. This was before they went to the large bands in there. Of course Basie was the first one there with the big band, and I was the second, and then I think Woody Herman came in, and then there was a whole slew, Teddy Powell, and even Red Nichols.
(Laughter)
Even.
Well, I mean you don't normally think of him with a big band.
Right. Right.
But he did have one in there. Oh, and then the Will Bradley band. They worked there.
How big was the Famous Door?
About the size of this boat.
(Laughter)
It was actually --
How many customers could they get in there with a big band?

Oh, they couldn't get more than 100 people in that place. It was the -- the basement level -- you know, one of those old brownstone houses in New York, and if you recall, you'd step down a couple of steps and then you'd

go into -- it wasn't the real basement. The ground floor was a couple of steps below street level, and they were kind of long and narrow. Well, now, that's the whole club.
