We jumped from jam sessions in Los Angeles to jam sessions in New York. Was there -- how did you get from Los Angeles to New York, and how and why? It just says in Chilton that you free lanced on the West Coast, then moved to New York formed first big band for three months residency at Paramount Hotel Grill, Spring, 1933, New York.

Well, actually we opened in November of '32 and we played on into '33, and we were there when Roosevelt turned the beer on. I remember they had big ads in the paper, "Free beer tonight," you know, and unfortunately our shipment got hijacked and we had a whole room full of people and no beer. But we finished out that engagement there, just a normal thing. And we were there, I think, three or four months. And we had had a -- oh, a CBS wire in there, radio, and we tried to, you know, float the band out on the road as an entity itself, but of course there really hadn't been enough exposure or there weren't enough people that gave a damn. I know that's the first time I met John Hammond. He came in, I didn't know who he was, and I said -- this guy came

in with a whole load of newspapers under his arm, you know, and very serious and attentive to everything that was going on, and came over and introduced himself. I think he was writing for The Melody Maker, the English paper, at that time. We had -- we were using all arrangements there in that band, which at the time, we had three trumpets and trombone, we had four brass and we had four saxophones, and believe it or not we had two piano players. The hotel insisted on having two piano players. Well, they had them, but we didn't let the other guy play, you know. He just, once in a while he'd -- but the manager was -- I guess he had been frightened to death by Ohman and Arden or something, and he had to have two pianos.
Do you remember who was in that band, that first band?

Yeah. Well, the guy that was making all the arrangements was Nathan Van Cleve, who later became quite a big heavy in the studios here, out in the West Coast, arranging. He was playing trumpet in the band. Johnny Dillard, Bob Kuzamano, and Doug Shoffner. That was the trumpet section. And the trombone player was Wally Baron. Let's see, Billy Speer was the baritone saxophone player, and Stu -- Stu, Stu, Stu, come on Stu, where are you -- Stu something was the tenor, and -- I've got a couple of blank faces there. Bill Long and Horace Diaz were the piano players. Bill King was the bass player. And Scoop Thompson was the guitar player.
I remembered more of those than I thought I was going to.
That's great.
That's a long time ago.
Yeah. So what was John Hammond's reaction to the band?

Oh, he wrote about our band, because we were playing all special arrangements, see, and this was unheard of around New York, except possibly the Goldkette band, when they would come in, or something like that, and he enthused in The Melody Maker about the band, and I remember we went over the play the musicians' ball, which was a command performance, you know, and we completely broke the place up. The musicians were screaming and hollering and of course that is the greatest accolade you can get in the world. It's nice from people, but when it comes from you know, your own group, it really means something.
That's great. So after the Paramount Hotel Grill was it the same band you took into the Park Central Hotel? You said you didn't go out of New York.

No. That band more or less fell -- Billy Gussack was the drummer. That band more or less fell apart. We went up and we played the New Kenmore Hotel in Albany, and then we went out to Dayton, Ohio, and Columbus, and the band just folded. We didn't have enough exposure to sustain ourselves and it came apart. The band at the Park

Central was an entirely different band, and we were there for six months. It was a long engagement. Ozzie Nelson had the job, and his manager, a fellow by the name of Milton Romer, took a liking to me and he said, 'You get a band together and we'll put you in here for one night. Ozzie's got a one nighter they're going to let him out for, and if you make a good impression we'll see about getting you in to follow him, you know, for the summer, the spring and the summer.' And fortunately, I guess I got the right guys together and we rehearsed enough, and we opened there. And we were there all of that -- it was almost six months.
Gee, that's great. Who were playing at the other hotels in New York around that time?

Well, let's see, Benny Goodman was trying to have a band at Billy Rose's joint on 53rd Street there, which is now the Hammerstein Theater, and he was having a rough time. I remember I even gave him a couple of arrangements. And he and Benny Carter -- and I remember this as clearly as though it was right now. Were rather disgusted with the reception of jazz, you know, or of big band jazz particularly, and jazz in general, and we sat one time at a table there at the Park Central, plotting a European -- we were all going to go. Benny had just come back from there. And we -- and Coleman Hawkins was still over there, and we were seriously plotting to go to Europe and set up shop.

But nothing ever came of it because Benny you know, managed to get going and he -- well, you know, a lot of things are talked of that never happen. But I remember talking about it. Of course every band in New York that was any kind of a band at all had a Benny Carter arrangement in the book. He wrote more arrangements that he was not paid for, because he had a copyist by the name of Jack Mazel, or Meizel, and every time Benny would make an arrangement Jack would make an extra copy for himself. Jack's room was piled to the ceiling with Benny Carter arrangements, and other people's arrangements. And he would go around and sell the arrangements. And so any band at all that was playing arrangements, like Benny Carter's, "Take My Word," or, "Lonesome Nights," as it was originally called, and let's see, his, "Nagasaki," and his, "Devil's," something or other, oh, they were around in all the books.
Did Benny know how they were getting in all those books?
I'm sure he didn't. I think he just didn't care. He's such a nice man that he figured, well, if he's making a couple of bucks, what the heck, you know.
You'd think he might have changed copyists. Well, it's nice his work was so popular. He's a great writer.
Well, you weren't anything unless you had a couple of Benny Carter arrangements in the book.
What other bands were playing in New York then, when you were there?

Well, at that time, let's see, the Casa Loma Band had come into the Roseland Ballroom and made quite a hit. Claude Hopkins' band was playing there also. And let's see, well, the inevitable Phil Spitalny and of course Freddie Martin, and Vincent Lopez. Let's see, I'm not sure, I think Hal Kemp was already gone from the Taft, but George Hall. And oh, there were -- this was before Shaw started his thing and it was before the Dorseys. The Dorseys, I think -- the Dorsey Brothers, that year, I think they came the following year, if I'm not mistaken, because Casa Loma was the -- I'm trying to remember who went into the Glenn Allen Casino first, whether it was the Dorsey Brothers or Casa Loma. Of course Casa Loma -- I'm inclined to think it might be the Casa Loma Band.
I think I have that somewhere in these notes, but I'll have to find it later.

Anyway, one of -- I'm sure the Casa Loma band didn't -- they may have gone in -- well, let's see, Jimmy Lunsford was around, too, although he wasn't -- the Cotton Club was still uptown, and I think he played there. I'm not sure. That was Harold Oxley's band. That was the one, the black band that the Mills organization didn't have. But yeah, -- let's see -- no, no, that's right, because Jimmy
Lunsford's band played opposite, they played at the Larchmont Casino when we played the Glenn Allen Casino, which was, I think, in '35, or '36.
Because Chilton.
It was '36.

Chilton has you going from -- let's see, the Paramount Hotel Grill in '33 to the following year, Park Central Hotel, '34, and then he says Glenn Allen Casino, Glen Island Hotel Roosevelt, New Orleans, et cetera.

Well, the Roosevelt Hotel came after, directly after, the Park Central. I remember we were there New Years Eve of '34 going into '35. And we were the first out of town band to play the room, and it was -- we used to play the dinner session in the Fountain Room, and Huey Long used to be in there every night for dinner. And he had these bodyguards around him, and they would sit, facing the backs of the chairs, looking around the rest of the room, and Huey would stuff his napkin in his neck and eat up a storm and send requests over to the band. He liked, 'Stars Fell on Alabama.' I don't know why, but that and that Jack Benny theme song, 'Love in Bloom.' And then we played the dinner session there, and then we'd have to pack the instruments up and go into the Blue Room, and we'd go through the lobby. And of course this was the first out of town band, and as we'd go through the lobby you could hear mutterings like, 'Damn yankees.' We weren't very popular there. At the time.
Some book says that Huey Long complained that the band was too loud and that the management told you to play softer and you wouldn't.
Oh, that's a lot of baloney. Huey never complained about anything. In fact he was a doll. In fact I was even his guest in the Unites States Senate later on.
Oh. I'm just trying to remember which --
I don't know where some of these things get started, but --
I think it was -- let's see.
The guy that did the complaining about being too loud was Seymour Weiss, the owner of the hotel.

I see. And how about -- I'm looking for which book I found it in. I think it was George Simon's book. Said the reason you left there was that they wanted you to play softer and you wouldn't, and so they set up some guys in the red light district, some guys in your band, and busted them, and then the band had to leave town. Is that right?

No. There was a setup of a kind, but the way it happened was Seymour Weiss called Milton Romer and said, 'Look, will you get this band out of here? They're driving me crazy.' So Milton went along, he called and said, 'Look, I've got a job for you in Miami Beach. Would you like
to work there?" And I said, "Oh, yeah." He said, "Well, give your notice." He was in cahoots with Weiss, see? There wasn't any job in Miami Beach. We gave our notice, and of course we were out.
Oh. And then where did you go?
We split. Incidentally, that band, the trumpet section's rather interesting. It was Chris Griffin, Eddie Sauter, and Tootie Camarata.
Gee.
And the -- we just split. That was the end of the band.
Who else was in it?

Well, Root Bigadack was the piano player. Les Cooper was the saxophone, first saxophone. Frank Llewellyn was the trombone player. And Fred Follensby was the tenor man. And Jack Henderson was the other alto man. And -- I'll tell you who came around there, and wanted to sit in, was Johnny -- he was quite a popular singer a few years back and he disappeared -- Johnny -- he's a guitar player. Now his last name's gone. Anyway --
Ray?

Oh, no, not Ray. I may think of it. Anyway, we had a guitar player by the name of Buford Turner, and it was a cooperative band, incidentally. So like I wasn't exactly responsible for what happened, you know. I was the guy up in front of it, but I mean we'd have our meetings, and when

they'd say don't play this and don't play that and the band would say no, we've got to play what we're going to play, and I'd say okay. You know. But that was the end of the big business cooperative band.
Well, Milton Romer booked your band, is that right? He was your manager or what?

He was the manager. In those days it was -- it wasn't much of a definition of who was a manager and who was a booker. The laws weren't too stringent about that. Like he did this directly. It wasn't done through any office. He still had Ozzie Nelson, who was very big at the time, you know. He had a commercial radio program and doing this thing.
Did you have any association with him after he pulled that on you in New Orleans?

Yeah, he actually did get me a job, later that year, in Miami Beach, with a five piece band, at a place called The Gangplank. Oh, it was a horrible band. They used local Miami musicians, and the only note that came out of the bass player was the slap, and it was terrible. But he -- one thing that happened there, during that time, I had gotten married, and it didn't work, and my -- that was my first wife and she was after me, so I decided I'd better go to Cuba. And --
Did you get married in Miami?

No, I was married in New York. We went back to New York after the New Orleans fiasco. And I had gone to Florida and Milton had gotten me this job, and in the meantime, I had gotten married. So I get word she's coming, and I said, 'Well, I'm going to Cuba.' There was a boat, an overnight boat, that used to leave for Havana, right out of Miami Beach there, and as the boat's pulling out, here she comes with her process server and I'm on the stern of the boat, and I'm hollering at her, 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for alimony.' I stayed in Havana for, oh, about the better part of four months.
Playing there?

No, I didn't play there. I kind of worked as a gigolo there. I used to -- these women would come in on the -- I met some guys around Sloppy Joe's bar there, and they'd come in on these cruise boats, you know, and you'd take them around and you'd get paid for it.
Was that fun?
Well, at the time it was fun, but that's not one of the proudest moments of my life, I'll tell you that.
So no music at all for four months. Did you listen to any music there? Was there any interesting music being played in Havana?
Not really. The rhythms were

interesting. But outside of a couple of flute players, the horn players weren't -- the greatest brass players, I mean trumpet players, are Mexican. And in Cuba the trumpet players were terrible. Whereas, they had tremendous guys that played flute and the clarinet. There were saxophone players there, but they'd more or less concentrate on the flute, because they weren't big bands then. They were smaller bands. But the rhythms were very exciting.
Is there any particular reason you know of why the good trumpet players are Mexican and not Cuban?
They don't have bull fights in Cuba.
I see.
You know, they have to have some pretty good trumpet players for the bull fights.
Yes. That's what Cat Anderson told me. His biggest inspiration was Rafael Mendez.
Oh.
So did you carry any Cuban rhythms back to your music in the United States?
Well, sure, I played maracas a little bit later, in Barney Bigard's Orchestra.
Of course, of course. Direct from Havana.
Uh-huh.
So when you got back from Cuba, where did you go?

I got my situation straightened away and I went back to New York and let's see, oh, somewhere in there I had been to California again. You say Cuba, see, we got all the way up to Cuba, which is '35, I was back in California in '32.
Oh, okay. Good.

And that was the time when I did a little extra work. Well, not extra work, but what they call sideline. I mean when they'd have an orchestra in a picture, the music was recorded by the studio orchestra, and then they would have -- I would be the guy standing there directing the band, you know. I did a little bit of that, and I got out of there just ahead of the earthquake.
Good.
The Long Beach earthquake.
What films -- I --
Oh, "Love and Hisses," and "Sally, Irene and Mary," and --
There's a new book out called, "Jazz in the Movies," and see those markers? Every one of those is a movie Charlie Barnet is in.
Really?
Yeah.
I didn't realize I was in that many.
That's what it says here.
They must be counting shorts, then, too.
Yeah, they do. They do.
Oh.
Including the Snader -- the things that became Snader Telescriptions, which were something else when they were made, right? The shorts that were made out at Universal?
Oh yeah.
They were made by Les Cowan, was that his name?
Oh, Will Cowan.
Oh, Will Cowan. Yeah.
That's his boat right there, the Alma Lee.
Oh.
And we see each other all the time.
Those were some great band shorts. He sold them to Snader, right?
No, Snader made their own.
Oh. Well, I say that because Duke made two for Cowan at Universal, which was in '49 and '50, and
they later showed up on Snader Telescriptions.

Well, they must have made some kind of a deal with Universal. But I remember I made one for him, or maybe two, I don't know. But we didn't do them at Universal. We did them at some other studio, and I remember the musicians' union was there, they couldn't figure out what was going on and they were very upset. They didn't know how to classify this type of endeavor. And they were watching the whole thing very closely. But that definitely was not made -- that was made directly for him.
For Snader.
Yeah.
Oh. Well it must have been later. Do you know what year that was?
Oh, that was in the -- oh, that's got to be in the late '40s.
Yeah. Yeah, that would fit. Late '40s or --
Because they were made for -- were they made for television or for these boxes in the bars?
Well, the firm was at least later known as Snader Telescriptions, so --
It seems to me they were originally made to be shown in bars.
Yeah, I think so too, in those little
machines.

Yes. So that could have been earlier, although I recall distinctly that Gene Roland Rowland was playing trumpet in the band that we made these things for, and I didn't know Gene, Gene never worked for me until late in -- the late '40s. So it's -- but now with Will Cowan, those were all done at Universal, and it was an entirely different thing.

Well, at one point, after we've gone through the chronological thing I want to go through and read off -- because these are not, unfortunately, chronological. These are alphabetical in order, and so we'll go through and --
Well, I wouldn't know the names of the shorts.
But you might remember them by date or something, or by circumstance.
I made quite a few for Will, I think.
Well, we'll check that.
Yeah, okay.
Later on. It's interesting, though. I mean there's this long list of references, after your name,
Yeah.
So when you came back to California you were sidelining in these films, "Sally, Irene and Mary," and -- I can't remember the other one you mentioned.
"Love and Hisses."
"Love and Hisses."
And, you know, trying to get something going musically, which there wasn't too much going on. Then I went back to New York, and that's when I organized the band that went into the Paramount.
And who was in that band?
I already gave you that. That was the one with Van Cleve and --
Oh, oh, oh. The Paramount Hotel.
The Paramount Hotel, yeah.
I'm sorry. I was thinking all of a sudden --
When you say the Paramount, you always think of the theater.
;Yeah. Okay. So we are chronologically now back to New York from Havana, right?
Yeah.
Okay. And was that -- the new band, in the spring of '35? Disbanded, moved to Hollywood, for short lived acting career. Now there's, "Love and Hisses," "Sally, Irene and Mary."
Yeah.
Okay. Reformed own band. Residencies at Glenn Island Casino and touring. Disbanded, then reformed band for residency at Famous Door.

Well, again Milton Romer to the front. He worked out of -- I guess he didn't give up on me. He got me the job at the Glen Island Casino. Now, I had this band that I'd been rehearsing, and you know, doing some work around, a little work around with it, and it was a travelling band, and by that, they weren't all Local 802 members. Excuse me. And when we had to go into the Glen Island Casino, the pay was so poor that you used to have to pay an extra 30 percent if you were a travelling band. And the pay was so poor that he says, "No, you've got to have an all New York band here or you're not going to make it." And so I had to get rid of a wonderful trumpet player by the name of Frank Amerall, and along with some other guys, and change it to an all New York band, and consequently when the band opened there, it was nothing like the band that we had had. And there was a lot of interference in that whole operation.
What kind?

Dictation of what was to be played and what was not to be played and who was going to make the arrangements and who was going to sing and who wasn't, and it wasn't a particularly happy engagement at all. And then we were standing in the shade of how great the Casa Loma Band had been, and the Dorsey Brothers, and -- there again, I could be wrong. I was more conscious of the Casa Loma Band. Maybe the Dorsey Brothers hadn't been there yet. I

don't know. It's possible they hadn't. But definitely the Casa Loma Band had really exploded there, and everything was, "Why don't you do it like the Casa Loma Band did?" You know this is pretty hard to live under. So that we finished out there and we were very happy.
You broadcast from there, didn't you?

Yes. We had a lot of air time. That was the whole idea. Sitting there with no money, was to get the air time. We were recording. We had made some records prior to that. We made some records in New Orleans for Bluebird. Eli Oberstein came through town with the portable unit and we recorded in some loft up there and we made six sides there, six or eight, I forget how many. Not any more than eight.
I think they're in here, right?
Yeah. Yeah.
They tell that story about recording circumstances, in those liner notes.

And then I had done some dates with -- up at Brunswick for some of those there, cover labels like Perfect and Mellotone, and the kind of dates where you just walk in and meet and carve up a stock orchestration or something and play it. In fact they had Benny Carter make some arrangements for some of those things, and oh, Joe Higgins was in charge of it. He just hit the ceiling. He

said, 'What are you trying to do to me?' 'All this doodley doop.' He said, 'We just want the melody.' And he cut -- in fact one of Benny Carter's arrangements, he just said, 'That, I won't even issue that.' And it was great, you know. And we had to come back and make the stock orchestration of the tune later, about a week later or something like that.
Is there, to your knowledge, a discography of your recordings?
I beg your pardon?
Is there, to your knowledge, a discography of your recordings, a complete list of everything you did?

Yeah, I've got a couple of them. One that is fairly up to date. It comes -- well, it doesn't have the last record in it. I think it does. It mentions it. '67 and '66. Yes, because it's got a mention of that Reader's Digest date I did, which it says unissued, which is not true. It was issued through Reader's Digest, but not in the stores. But that's actually the last record date. Yeah, this is, oh it's a book, I'd say, about three quarters of an inch thick, and it's got everything listed, and it's pretty thorough. The personnel is all wrong in a lot of things, but -- and then of course Leonard had a discography that was up to a certain year. And then there's another one that comes in two volumes that only goes up as far as '42.
Is that more accurate?
No, it's just as bad.
What is the best one that's been done, do you think?

Well, there really isn't any best one. It's -- they all suffer from the same thing, and that is inaccuracy in personnel. They're very good when it comes to, oh, something like, Bluebird, or recent years, you know. But when it gets back there, I guess the records weren't kept very well and they don't know who was on those dates. And of course I have only been consulted about things like that, oh rarely, maybe two or three times. I probably wasn't much help either, you know, because it sort of fades into a was it that date or was it this date. It's very hard to nail it down.
Yeah. Where are they published and by whom, the discographies?

Well, one guy is in Florida. He's also putting out bootleg records at this time. And this other is a regular, handsomely bound, there's two books, they're quite thick, and I got them -- I noticed them advertised in one of the book things that we get in the mail, and it has every band that ever recorded anything, except that it does not cover jazz. They do not cover Duke in there, they do not cover Basie. In other words, what they call

out and out jazz bands. They -- it also says in there that these have been covered very thoroughly elsewhere. But there's all sorts of bands there. Did you know that the guy that made the most records of anybody, do you know what his name is? The orchestra? Bob Haring, H-a-r-i-n-g.
I never heard of him.
There's something like 40 pages of things that were recorded under his name. I knew of him, vaguely. I never met him. But I was looking through this the other day and I couldn't believe this.
I'll be darned.
However, those, there again, you'll see big gaps in there. Unknown, unknown, you know. And it's --
Who is the guy in Florida who has done one? His is the one that goes to '42?
No, he goes right up to today. Up till through '67. I can't tell you his name offhand, but besides, I just said he's putting out bootleg records, and I don't --
This material is kept confidential. As confidential as you want it to be. It's up to you what happens to this material.
I really don't remember his name. I could supply it to you, but I don't have it --
It would be interesting to know. And
also know that the personnel was not --

Well, Leonard Feather had one out, called, "The Hot Discography," or something like that, and I don't believe it went any further than maybe in the mid-'40s or something like that. I think it was his first thing he put out. Now, he may have updated it.
Not to my knowledge. I don't think so. Was it more accurate than these others?

It was pretty accurate, yeah. However, when you get back in the murky areas, you get back too far, he suffers from the same thing, probably lack of records on the part of the recording companies, plus the fact that people have passed on and there isn't anybody to ask. The same thing you're having the problem with me, I can't remember the name of this guy when I know him very well, you know, or that guy.
Well, at least we have the names of the labels that you recorded for during that period. So --

When you recorded for Brunswick there you had no idea what label you were on, because you might be on Perfect Records in one town, Mellotone in another, and Vocalion in another, and Auriole in another. They had all of these multiple labels, so that there was no way of telling. And it was all the same date. So if you called a record company, to me, it really wouldn't mean much, unless it was one of the big three of the time, you know, like Victor, Columbia and Decca, or something like that.
Uh-huh. So you were back in New York. At what point did you meet Duke? This is about now the time when you did your maracas.
Well, I met Duke when he was -- he opened at the Cotton Club, downtown.
Uh-huh.

And I used to be up there, oh, three or four nights a week. And we got to talking to him, and of course I knew the guys in his band before I knew him, and we became good friends, as good a friend as anybody was ever able to be with Duke. Now, Duke, God bless him, he's a wonderful man, but very few people ever really knew where they were with Duke. I don't mean that he would put up with you if he disliked you, but there's very few people that ever really got close to Duke. He -- I think he did sort of take a fatherly interest in me, though, because he was always very nice to me, and goodness knows, later on, when I wanted to throw a party, I mean he came and played the party, and that was it. He said, 'Forget it.'
Well, he liked you very, very much. I mean there was a closeness that I saw, but that of course was later.
But do you know what I'm trying to say, Pat, is he was a very hard man to know where you actually stood with him.
I know.
I mean you knew he didn't dislike you, you know, he liked you, but you weren't quite sure whether he was just putting up with you or -- I can't even put it into words.

Again to skip some time, something I've wanted to ask you for a long time, and that is about that night at the Grove in Los Angeles, I think it was 1972, when in his dressing room you and he got into a big discussion about emotion in music.
Oh, yes. Yeah.

And which that poor, dear man, Bill Struthers, thought he had recorded, Bill Struthers being a disc jockey on KPFK here, and it turned out that it wasn't recorded, which is another funny story. But do you feel that Duke believed where he was arguing from that night? Because Duke took the standpoint that --
That there was no place for emotion in music.

Right. And you said that not only did you absolutely disagree with him, but that you could not believe that he felt that way from listefning to Ellington music. And it went on from there and it got to be a very heated argument.
Well, it wasn't really that. It was
never to the point of ill feelings or anything like that.
No, but there were raised voices. But do you believe that Duke believed what he was saying, or do you think that Duke was merely being a provocateur?

No, I believe that he -- at that point in his life, I believe that he really believed what he was saying. Now, there may have been a question of semantics, semantics involved there. Because as I recall I agreed with him on this point. I said a person that gets overly emotional and gets high, I mean, and really thinks he's blowing up a storm probably isn't.
Right.

Now, I went that way. But I said, 'When you say that there is no emotion at all, should be no emotion whatsoever in music,' I said, 'I have to disagree with you.' And then he started citing the symphonies, how there's -- and I said, 'Well, there again, those things have to be played a certain way and they're played the same way every time, and you can't tell me that a person, even in a symphony, doesn't feel better one night than maybe on some other night.' Where it wouldn't be evidence, you know, of any histrionics in his playing, but possibly the conductor or the people he plays with would notice it. Maybe he was more or less inspired. And I said, 'With your own band,' I said, 'The greatest example of it in the world.' I said, 'What happened with Paul
Gonsalves in --
Newport?

Newport. And the whole band. I said, "You can't tell me that the emotion didn't raise that band." "Oh," he said -- in other words, it wasn't so much an argument as I think possibly Duke was disapproving of people that get loaded or get high on something and go on to play and think that they're helping their playing and --

Yeah, but he went further -- besides that, he said that if you get emotional about your music then you lose control of it and you have to have control of it in order to evoke emotion in the listener. And if you're involved in your emotions then you're not in control and you're not going to be concerned with the effect of the music on the listener.
Well, I think he's probably right in that context.
You said --

If you get overly exuberant in your playing, you get excited, you have a tendency to maybe over-estimate your ability and attempt things that you wouldn't normally attempt. On the other hand, I mean, some wonderful things have happened out of things like that.
But you're saying overly emotional but Duke said no emotion.
He said no emotion. No, I don't agree with that.

But do you think he really meant it, because you said that you felt that emotion could very often be a wonderful inspiration, and Duke said absolutely not. Do you think that he was just arguing, taking a different point of view, or do you think he really believed that? I found it hard to believe that he really believed it.

I thought he believed that, and I had reasons for it, for believing that he did believe it. Now, I'm not saying this derogatorily or anything, but don't forget, we were looking at a man in his 70s at that time.
Uh-huh.

A lot of things about Duke had changed. The band had changed considerably. And I think that his thinking about the band, the very thing, the kind of things the band was playing, along those times -- along about that time, were -- well, some of them, so far as I'm concerned, didn't make it. I felt cheated. Now, this could have been by the fact that, you know, maybe Johnny's gone and Strayhorn was gone, and the trumpet section was kind of in an uproar back there. And Duke was more or less getting in his ivory tower. I mean he'd sit up in the room there, all by himself, and I had a feeling that he was withdrawn a little bit, from the Duke that I had known, you know, in previous years. However,
who's going to fault that? Everybody gets old.
Sure.

And I guess as you get older you become very firmly fixed with ideas. I find myself becoming very dogmatic about certain things now that maybe before I would be hanging on a cliff, yes I will, no I won't, and now I have pretty definite opinions about a lot of things that I didn't have before. So I think that had a lot to do with it. That's what I had attributed it to. I've told this a lot -- of course when anybody says we got into an argument, no.
I don't mean a hostile argument, but I mean a spirited argument.
Oh, It was spirited.
A spirited discussion. You were taking two different points of view very strongly.
Yeah.

One of the things that you probably don't know -- I just told Bill Struther the other day, that you know he had come back to get an interview with Duke, and when you and Duke got into this he turned his tape recorder on, and I thought, 'Oh, great. He has a record of this, because I'd like to listen to this again.' After Duke had to go onstage for the next show --
What'd he do, erase it accidentally?
No. He said to me, he says, 'Patty,

I don't want that ever to be broadcast. What just went on in here," he said, "must never be broadcast." He said, "Get that tape." I said, "I can't get that tape from that man. That man has something that nobody has, what just went on in there." He says, "Your assignment is to get that tape. I don't want it broadcast." And so I went out looking for Bill Struther in the Grove, and he'd gone. He took his tape and went home. And so I figured that I'd wait until the next morning and try to figure out something, went home worrying about it. The first thing in the morning -- because Duke told me I was to deliver the tape to the hotel the next day -- the first thing in the morning I was trying to figure out what to say to Bill Struther, and the phone rang and it was Bill Struther, and he said, "The most horrible thing has happened. I couldn't wait to play that tape again this morning. I put it on, it's blank." I swore -- I told Duke --
That's the Ellington magic.

Yeah, yeah. I remember I met him in

No, I never got in the service.

Well, I don't know. They kept calling me back and calling me back, but they had me in various -- I was in 1-A three times, and on every occasion I was -- something happened. "Well, we don't have to tell you what to do. You know the routine."
Well, for how long a period of time did this go on?
Well, that's over a period of a couple of years.
It really messed up any plans you might make.

Well, you couldn't. That's why I disbanded the band and came out to California. Oh, that's Buck and Bubbles.

Well, we had been in there, we're waiting. We had been up all night, and we're in there and they were doing some connecting things, you know, and we're sitting there, and we're waiting for Benny, and we were called at 8:00 o'clock in the morning, and that's makeup at 7:30, and we're waiting and we're waiting and we're waiting, and no Goodman. And finally they call his house. "Well, Mr. Goodman is having breakfast." Well, then, "Mr. Goodman will be there pretty soon." Well, to make a long story short, Benny

comes walking in around 11:30. By now, Tommy's fuse is lit. He's so mad he cannot be contained, you know, and one word led to another and we started in, you know. And we played it, it was a thing in unison, and we finished the thing. Little rings, we were doing. And Benny just kept on playing, like that, so Tommy said, "All right, Benny. We all know how good you play. Now come on, let's do this and get out of here. We've been here all morning." And one word led to another. Tommy threw his trombone at me and I caught it, and he took his glasses off and he started for Benny. So I got Pops over and I'm talking to him, and I see Emil go over and he gets the trumpet and he pulls the slide out about an inch, or an inch and a half or something. we start the thing again, and Louis's just as sharp as he was before. In other words, that's the way he heard it, and moving the slide didn't mean a thing.
There's a picture here from that film. Is there anything there that --

Yeah.
