We were along about '37, before we got into your movies, and you'd been to the Glenn Island Casino and you were in New York. You talked about Duke at the Cotton Club and Andy Gibson writing for your band, right?

That's right. I had this band that I was rehearsing which was Ellingtonized. In other words it was in the direction of the Ellington approach to music. And of course we still had a lot of problems getting decent jobs. And we went out to the New Penn Club, right outside of Pittsburgh, which also had a broadcast wire, a national broadcast wire, because that was the big thing in those days.

You had to get on the air, and records really weren't that important, which is strange. I mean they were important in a sense, but as compared to today, it was like night and day. The live broadcasts were the things that brought people in.
At that point were records licensed for radio broadcast? They weren't were they? You had to --

Well, this is the thing that Fred Waring fought for years and got nowhere. But the fact remains that a record is a form of publication. For example, you can get in ASCAP if you've got a record of a tune, whether you have anything printed or not. You say here's the record. They recognize that as a form of publication. And therefore, if you own the -- if you bought the record you can do anything you want with it. Now, Fred was trying to say that everybody should get paid when they played the record on the radio. Well, there weren't all these disc jockeys, then. There were a few big ones like Martin Block and Al Jarvis out on the coast, and -- but nothing like today. The whole thing was live broadcasts. You've heard Steve Allen do his wonderful, "And now from atop the So-and-So Roof in Downtown Minneapolis," well, this was the way it was. From all over the country you got live broadcasts. Every night from, oh, 10:30, 11:00 o'clock on, even earlier. And there just -- there wasn't any substitute. Records alone wouldn't do it in those days.
Well, didn't it work in a way that if
you were heard on the radio a lot then there became a demand for you and then you got bookings?

That's true. So consequently, any of these jobs you could get where you got radio time, like some of the biggest bands in the business took jobs in hotels and places, clubs that had radio time for unbelievably low money, because they would recoup it by going out on the road and then capitalizing on this exposure. So when we got to the New Penn, I had never heard of the New Penn, and as far as I'm concerned I hope I never hear of it again. It was outside on the -- it was like a roadhouse. And I think the Mafia owned it or something, because it was a rough place. But they had the wire. That was where I first met Billy May. We were having a rehearsal again, and here was this guy waiting there, and his shoes were cut out at the side to make it more comfortable, and he said, 'I've got an arrangement I'd like to have you try.' I told him the same thing, 'As soon as we finish what we're doing here I'll be happy to try it.' So we passed the arrangement out and the guys in the band, it was in the afternoon and they wanted to get out. They started groaning and I said, 'Well, let's try the arrangement.' We passed the arrangement out, and they were real drug and bored, and they leaned back and they got through about the first eight bars of the arrangement and they all came up in their seats and they were looking at the music, and Mr. Billy May was in.
Wow.

And of course we went to the Famous Door shortly after that, and I sent for Billy. I said, "I want you to come in and arrange for me," you know. Oh, it was a ridiculous deal. Something like $15.00 an arrangement or something like that. And Billy was not playing in the band, he was just writing for it. He and Andy Gibson and Billy Moore, Jr., William Moore, Jr. Oh, and there was another guy by the name of Bud Estes who -- they were all writing for the band. Benny Carter contributed a couple of things. But we were -- Benny was busy elsewhere and these guys were all writing in the vein that we were exploring. Billy Moore had a tendency, and Estes, had a tendency to lean a little more toward the Lunceford approach, and of course Andy Gibson was strictly in the Duke groove, and Billy was -- he was back and forth between the two. But it made a nice lineup of arrangers, and we got some interesting scores. I had Billy in New York, and I heard that Benny Goodman -- Benny Goodman, we were playing the Famous Door, and one of the music publishers tipped me off that Benny Goodman was after Billy May, he was trying to find him. So I moved Billy. I had a suite at the Park Central Hotel, and I said, "Billy, why don't you come on and move in with me." And we had -- so Billy moved in there and we actually had him hidden. We wouldn't let him out of the room. "Oh, anything

you want, order, room service. Just keep writing." And we had him hidden from Benny. Of course at that time Benny was making so much money I couldn't have kept Billy at all. And we were successfully able to keep him away from Benny Goodman, which -- well, maybe I did him a favor.
How do you mean?
Well, I don't think they would have gotten along very well.
Probably not. So how long did Billy live with you, then, in order to keep him?
Oh, about three months. By that time Benny had gotten somebody else to arrange for him. I don't know who it was, but he wasn't looking for an arranger anymore.
Who was in the band when you opened at the Famous Door?

Well, actually there were -- well, we had a wonderful piano player by the name of Nat Jaffe, who was -- he was like Tatum, you know. He wasn't the greatest band piano player in the world, but he had a technique like Art's. I mean he was just fantastic. And the rest of the guys in the band were -- there weren't really any stars. Bobby Burnett was in that band, a trumpet player who was with me for quite awhile after that, there, and later. And we really didn't have -- it was more or less of a team effort, rather than a bunch of -- there weren't any stars, so as to speak, outside of possibly Jaffe and Bob Burnett. We did have a very

singular person by the name of Johnny Mendel, not Mandel, but Johnny Mendel, out of Chicago. He was -- that wasn't his real name. He was Polish, and he was one of the sole remaining guys that knew how to growl and use a plunger. And he was in the band. And he played a particularly beautiful solo on a thing that Barney Bigard wrote, called, "Meant For a Lost Love." It's a muted solo with a harmon mute the -- it's one of the prettiest things. I still play it every now and then, when I think of it, because it's so pretty, what Johnny Mendel played on that. But he was kind of a crotchety old man then, I mean, anyway. You know, he was much older than all of us, and -- but nevertheless, the band was enthusiastic. That's the whole thing. And they imparted this to the people, and we had good arrangements, and that was about the size of it. And things went along. We went into the Paramount Theater, my first time in the Paramount Theater, with Dorothy Lamour and Mischa Auer, and that was our first of quite a few Paramount engagements. And that was when we had to press Billy into service as a trumpet player. By that time we had a first trumpet player by the name of Charlie Huffine, and Charlie got a bad lip or got sick, I don't know, or he didn't show up, I don't know. For some reason he wasn't there. And I said, "You play trumpet, " to Billy. I said, "You've got to step in there." Well, as far as I know he hadn't touched the trumpet the whole time he was in New York. I know he didn't touch it because we were living together. And he got the trumpet and he took over the first

trumpet chair and played it unbelievably well. Which of course he wasn't a first trumpet player, but he knew all the charts because he'd written them. And what he couldn't do he'd say, "You play that," you know, and that's when Billy became actually a playing arranger with my band. But in fact that's when we went to four trumpets, because we'd only had three up to that point with that band. And, oh, a couple of years later Glenn Miller stole Billy from me, but he did it by accident. Actually this is very funny. He told his manager, he said, "Find out the guy that's playing that jazz with Charlie Barnett. I want him." Well, actually it was Bob Burnett that was playing all the jazz, and the guy happened to come in when Billy was playing one of his three jazz solos, and Glenn hired Billy instead of Bob, which actually, although I love Bob dearly, and he was you know, pretty much a part of everything, to lose Billy then was quite a loss, because Billy had been the backbone of the arranging. He had written "Cherokee," and "Pompton Turnpike," and a lot of the other records of that time. That They were most important to us, and I hated to lose him. But I lost him on a fluke.
Glenn Miller could pay a lot more?
Oh, sure. Glenn was already very big.
I've read a lot of references to your band's material in which it says you played a lot of Duke's arrangements, but you played very few of Duke's actual
arrangements.
No, we didn't play his arrangements. We played his tunes.

Yeah, because as Duke says, in, "Music is My Mistress," he said, "Charlie Barnet has always been a wonderful friend to me, because of his musicianship, good judgment and good taste. He has always had people working for him whose potential was immense," and he mentions the people, "and at the same time he constantly bolstered my ego by playing a book almost full of our compositions. The arrangements of our things, no copycat versions, were done to fit the Charlie Barnet Band, and they were suitable for whatever occasion he played." It's as though, I feel, Duke wanted to set the record straight, because of all --

Well, I'll tell you, Pat, why that happened. You see, after the Palomar fire in 1939, there was an erroneous rumor that got around that Duke came to our rescue and gave us a whole bunch of arrangements, you know, to get restarted, because we'd lost the whole library and everything. Actually, he didn't give us any arrangements, because I don't even think he knew about the fire or knew of our predicament. The guy that did give us some arrangements was Count Basie. Because Basie was supposed to follow us in and he was in the same boat with us. He came all the way out to California to open and there was no place to open. And he was booked in for four weeks, so his managers were in a

scramble to get him booked, and here we were with no instruments, no library, and we had jobs to go to, but it was a question of what are we going to play. Now fortunately that band had been together for so long with the same personnel, we had so many head arrangements and the guys could remember all the arrangements. We went all the way across the country, back to Boston, to the Southland Cafe, which took about a month to get there, and we never had a music stand in front of anybody the whole trip. In the meantime the arrangers were busy and -- writing the -- at first they were starting to send them. I said, "Don't send them, we're doing fine. We haven't got time to rehearse anyway. We'll get there. Just have them in Boston and then we'll do it there." So we actually played that whole trip with no music, and this gassed a lot of people. They'd look at the band, you know, and there's no music. But these guys knew everything. We had a tremendous amount of head arrangements anyway, and the same personnel, plus the fact that they were able to remember enough of a lot of the things that were written down that they could play them.
Well, I read somewhere that a lot of band leaders sent you arrangements when they heard about your predicament. Basie was the only one?
Basie was the only one.
What did you do for instruments instantly?

We all went out and bought new instruments. And there was a guy by the name of Carlos Gastell, who was running -- later he was the manager of Nat Cole and Peggy Lee and Mel Torme and Nellie Lutcher and all that.
I knew him then.

And Carlos, that's the first time I met him, he was running a ballroom called the Domar Ballroom, down at one of the beaches, Hermosa or someplace right there, and we had to find a place to play, to try out our new instruments and to find out how much we remembered. He said, 'I'll take the band.' So he put us in there and we went through, and I said, 'Hey, we've got enough. We can go. We don't have to worry about anything.' And of course Carlos and I later became real great friends. In fact we were in business together for a short time. One time I decided I wanted out of the music business and went to work with him as a personal manager.
When was that?

Oh, that was in '49, when I broke the '49 band up, which is another story, why I did that. But I wanted out of the music business for awhile, but I went with him and I stayed with him about six months, six, seven months, just for something to do, to see if I'd like it. I didn't like it. Because you not only have your own troubles, you have everybody else's troubles. And I have the greatest respect
for a successful personal manager, because he must go through hell.
Yeah, it ain't easy.
But Carlos and I became long and fast friends there ever after, and I really felt -- I can't remember feeling any worse when anybody went than I did when Carlos went.
I know, he was a very well liked person.
You know those articles in the Reader's Digest, the most unforgettable character? He would be one of those.
Did you ever see him in anything besides those wild Hawaiian shirts?
I've seen Carlos under every possible situation.
Did he own an unprinted shirt or a coat? I never saw him wear anything but those loud Hawaiian shirts.

Oh, he owned them, but Carlos was a sweat machine. Sweat would pour off him all times of the day, all seasons. He just was in a continual perspiration. He -- of course as you know, Carlos was rather on the stout side, and you know he wouldn't eat until midnight or 11:00 o'clock, and then he'd eat a tremendous meal and then go to bed. But I've never seen --I used to say "Carlos, who has the handkerchief
concession with you?" Because he was always in a sweat. A very nervous man, a chain smoker. But if he was on your side, boy, you had somebody on your side.
Uh-huh. I know.
He's the only man in my life that I ever gave power of attorney to.
That says something strong.
That's true.
The fire at the Palomar, that started in radio equipment, is that correct?
No, it started right on the bandstand.
How?

Well, they had these draperies. It had been terrifically hot in L.A., you know, up in the hundreds, and everything was dried out, and these -- nowadays, of course, you couldn't hang draperies without the Fire Department checking them, you know, for being fireproof. And we had these huge electric light bulbs in the footlights back of there, and these curtains would sag, so one of them was touching one of these lights, and it just went phfffft, like that, and we were actually in the place. We were off the bandstand at the time, taking an intermission. And the fire went up so fast it was just like it exploded. It just went whoosh, like that, and the whole -- the only guy that got his instrument off was the bass player, who had laid it down on the front edge of the

apron. Because I always liked the bass up close to me, up front. Because as far as I'm concerned that's where it all comes from, the bass. Everything that's happening. And he was able to -- he got singed a little bit, but he got it off. Everything else was gone, all the instruments, all the music. We even had the trunk with the scores in it, because we were leaving. It was the next to the last night. And we had the trunk down there, all the scores that we had put into the band. Well, we had been gone from New York, maybe like three months. They were all in the trunk, and they went up too. So it was just like starting from scratch. But I always figured maybe somebody did me a favor there, because I had a whole mixed up bag of arrangements, and maybe they started me off, you know, with a clean slate, and I got rid of a lot of stuff that I shouldn't have been playing. And the ones that were important we were able to recreate.
Do you remember what specific numbers Basie gave you?

Yeah. "Moonlight Serenade", was one of them. Actually he gave us six arrangements that he thought that we could use, because see he knew that we had a lot of jazz head arrangements and everything. We were all right in that department. He gave us, "Moonlight Serenade." I can't remember the others, but they were pop tunes. You know. None with vocals, but they were ballads, you know, done very nicely, and --
Arranged by whom? Do you remember?
Well, actually by -- some of them were done by a guy that was playing in our band, Skippy Martin.
Oh.

He had written quite a bit for the Basie Band back in New York. And I don't know who made the others. I know that Skippy made a couple of them. But they came in quite handy when we regrouped, you know, and -- of course the "Moonlight Serenade" was a far cry from the Glenn Miller version.
I imagine. Have we skipped anything between the -- between '37 and '39?
Well, not really. I mean we had, you know, a rather haphazard existence until the Famous Door. It was an in and out situation.
Was the Famous Door after the Palomar?
No, before.
So it was -- was it essentially the same band from the Famous Door that got to the Palomar?

Yeah, it was the same band, with you know, a few minor changes. We had a different drummer, and there had been a couple of changes, one change in the trumpet section and one in the saxophone section, oh, and one in the trombone section. We had gotten Lyle, "Spud" Murphy, for the first trombone, which we needed badly, because none of the

guys we had in the Famous Door was really a first trombone player and Spud was. And we had strengthened the trumpet section by adding Johnnie Owens, and we had Ray Michaels playing drums, rather than Wes Dean, who was in the Famous Door band. But basically it was the same band, and they'd been together a long time, you know as bands go.
Did Spud Murphy write for your band then?
No. That's a different Spud Murphy.
Oh.
The one that does the writing is a saxophone player.
Oh.
Oh, incidentally, when I started my first band, you know, going -- before the Paramount, I bought Jan Garber's library for twenty bucks, when he changed over to the Guy Lombardo thing?
Uh-huh.

And Spud had written most of those arrangements. It was a sort of a pseudo-swing band, you know. It wasn't the -- the only part was that Spud never wrote any parts for himself, because he had them in his head, having written the arrangements. And I got all of these arrangements. I was able to -- oh, there must have been a couple of hundred arrangements. There was a trunk full of
music and -- every one -- I got maybe 25 arrangements out of there that were playable, because -- that Spud hadn't written.
That's funny. Didn't he also write for Benny Goodman?

Yes, he wrote for Benny Goodman. He wrote for a lot of people. Spud was a very good arranger. He's still around, up in the union. He has some capacity up there, I don't know exactly what. He's on one of the boards or committees, one of the elder statesmen.
Yeah. I think he's about 70 by now.
He would have to be.
Yeah. So after the Palomar you went back --

To the Southland. Well, one nighted across the country, to the Southland Cafe in Boston, and then we did a lot of rehearsing and put all the new charts in, and got back to a more disciplined way of playing, because we were romping pretty good on that trip, as you can imagine, you know, with mostly head arrangements and -- but I was lucky that I had a band that had that many head arrangements, because otherwise we'd have been out of business.
For sure. Chilton mentions that you once depped -- that must be a British term for subbed -- on alto for Otto Hardwick, with Duke Ellington on the 6th of March, 1943.
Yes.
What happened?

This was at the Casa Manana. In fact I have a picture of that. A picture of me sitting in the Ellington section with Johnny Hodges on one side and Harry Carney on the other and the other guys. The Ellington Band and my band -- Joe Zuka, who had the Casa Manana, I was sort of the house band in there, you know, and he said, 'I've got Duke Ellington coming in,' he said, 'I'm going to have you both here for the weekend.' I said, 'Oh, great, wonderful.' So now we're plotting backstage, we're going to have to subdue them, so we adopted a policy we were going to get them drunk. Now, they had the Red Callendar Trio to play while the bands were changing position on the stage, because there was only room for one band on the stage. So Toby, you know, he went pretty good -- that's Otto Hardwick -- and he got a little out of it, and Duke came out there just as I was giving him a drink, you know, and he looked at me, and if looks could kill I would have gone right through the floor. He says, 'So.' Okay. So I got real guilty. I said, 'Gee.' Toby was -- he really couldn't go out. He had had it. So I went out and I said, 'Boss, can I help you out here a little bit?' And he says, 'Go ahead, sit down.' And so I wound up playing the whole set with Duke that night.
That was nice.

And we had a rousing finale with both bands on stage and everybody, a whole bunch of musicians, Wingy Manone jumped up there, Corky Corcoran, I mean everybody in the joint. I've got a picture of this, home.
It must be fabulous.

Everybody playing, and I think we were playing "C Jam Blues." I don't know. Maybe that was before "C Jam Blues." We were playing some kind of blues. And we had a ball. And Joe -- you know who played most of the night? Red Callendar. Because the bands would get together in the back and they were all drinking together and everything, and Joe Zuka came back and he said, "I'm paying for two big bands, what have I got? I've got a stinking trio out here playing. Now get somebody on this bandstand," you know. And it was really a rather humorous situation. That band room was just like a nightclub.
It sounds like a very special night.
It was.
The 6th of March, 1943. Okay. You haven't mentioned clarinet at all.
Clarinet?
Uh-huh.
Oh, I very seldom used the clarinet. I did on one record, "Lament For A Lost Love," but not as a -- I didn't play any solos. I played -- they had the traditional

"Mood Indigo" trio there, the muted trombone and trumpet and the sub-tone clarinet. I played that on it, but I never played any solos on clarinet, because to be very frank, I was very awkward on the instrument and I didn't like it, I didn't like to play it, and I didn't play it very well, and I always figured there was other guys around, you know, could do a lot better. I just forgot about it, but once in a while I'd get pressed into service, because maybe Billy or Andy had those guys doing something else and they needed a clarinet for an effect or something like that. That would be the only way I would use the clarinet.

In going through all of the jazz history books there are an enormous number of major musicians who mentioned having played with Charlie Barnet. It is absolutely phenomenal. All of the really important stars and contributors to jazz who have been through your bands. You picked some very fine people.

Well, Pat, you know, to my own amazement, I had a tablet like you've got there, and made out my own list, and I was amazed. But I tell you, I think it isn't a question that I found them so much as they maybe found me, just as much as I found them, maybe moreso. Because we had a freedom of expression in our band that the Dorseys, neither one of them, didn't have, and certainly Benny Goodman didn't have it. I mean he was quite a taskmaster, and I always had

a, you know, like go ahead and do your own thing, whatever you want to do, but be able to play, that's all I ask of you. There was no fingernail inspection or shined shoes or -- I more or less, if they fit in with the way we they were doing, they stayed. If they didn't they left. But musicians, you know, they have a way of finding situations like that. They would hear about it. That's why I say, as many or more of them found me than I found them. And I was very fortunate that way, because I had a bunch of wonderful blowers in that band, all kinds, all kinds of instruments.
Yeah, well what, Red Norvo, right?

Well, Red and I, you know, actually had an orchestra together. When neither one of us could get steady work. When he got the job he'd stand in front of the band, and usually that was when Mildred Bailey would work, he'd -- and he'd do his bit with the xylophone, and I would sit down and play saxophone in the section. And when it was my job, Red would play piano. But it was the same band.
Who was in that band?

Oh, there was -- let's see, there was a trombone player by the name of Russ Jenner. Eddie Sauter. Chris Griffin. Oh, a wonderful trumpet player who later made some records with Red. Oh, I can't think of his name. Bob White was a drummer. It was a five brass, four saxophone band. I can't really recall. It gets a little blurred there

because I can't even tell you who else was in the saxophone section, except I think -- I'm not sure, but I think that Hymie Schertzer was in that band. I could be wrong, but I seem to remember him. Because that was a -- it was a very loose relationship. In other words, jobs weren't that often. We'd play something with Mildred, and then maybe I'd get a few one nighters and we'd load in the automobiles and take off and play them and come back. And sometimes the guys that played, like Mildred's jobs were maybe in a theater in Newark or something, the guys that played that wouldn't go play the one nighters, so we had to substitute. But contrary to what Eddie Sauter says, one thing he says is that I took the band up to Bar Harbor, Maine and got fired for playing undanceable music. It wasn't me. It was Red Norvo that took the band up there, and I wasn't even in the band. In one of the books this is a quotation. Because I have never been in Bar Harbor in my life, so I couldn't have -- that's one atrocity that I wasn't responsible for.
Okay, we got that one straightened out. How about Howard McGee, how did he happen to get in your band?
Well, we needed a trumpet player and Howard's a good trumpet player, and so we hired him.
That was where?
That was in New York. I think that was about '43, maybe early '44, and Howard wrote a couple of

charts for us. One of them we recorded, it was called, "Strolling". And he was a much more modern style trumpet player than Peanuts Holland, and this was an attempt in a way, you know, to have more of a variety of styles of trumpet players, because Peanuts was the traditional type trumpeter.
They were in the band at the same time?
Oh, yeah.
That's what I thought.

He and Al Killian. Al Killian was still there part of the time. But at that time I think we were using five trumpets, which it seems to me we were. Anyway, the reason for it was we wanted a guy that was playing in a more modern idiom. He was into the Dizzy Gillespie bag and --
Yeah, a bopper.
Yeah. And so we got Howard.
How long was he in the band?
Well, he was with the band until I just couldn't stand these -- when I broke the band up on account of these appearances before the draft board, I just -- it was really unnerving, you know.
Sure.
It was like somebody -- you're standing on a rug and waiting for somebody to pull it out from underneath you. So it wasn't that he got fired. I just disbanded the

whole band. And of course Howard went on, he made quite a mark for himself. Unfortunately he was ill with some things that a lot of the guys got into, which was a shame, because I always thought that Howard could play as good as anybody when he was right. He's still here, though.
Yeah.
And that's --
Yeah, I saw him conducting last year, in Los Angeles.
Well, good.
I don't know whether he's playing much, but --
Well, of course Howard's got to be up there now. We're talking back '43, here we are in '78. This is 35 years ago.
Dizzy's still playing, though.
Oh, yes, he is.
Dizzy was in your band very briefly, right?
Yeah. And you know what Dizzy played with me? Dizzy played first trumpet.
Oh, yeah? No, I didn't know that. I just knew he'd played for you.
Well, I had a job to go on the road, and I didn't have a trumpet section. You know, it was

scuffling time and we were going to play at the -- some hotel, the Netherlands Plaza or someplace in Cincinnati. So I got ahold of Dizzy, I said, "Hey, you want to make this trip?" He said, "Yeah, sure." I said, "Well, John, we need another trumpet player, too. You got anybody in mind?" He said, "How about Joe Guy?" I said, "Okay. I don't know him, but if you --," He said, "Yeah, he'll be fine." I said, "There's only one thing, John, you've got to play first trumpet." He said, "I'll play it." And he did. He did a heck of a job.
Wow. That was right after he left Calloway, right?
Yeah. Yeah. And that was a place where I -- you know, Cincinnati's pretty close to the jumping off place as far as that kind of stuff -- mixed bands are concerned.
Was there a problem?

The committee came over and they said -- the same curiosity that I had run into. Not antagonism, but like how can you -- how do you -- fine, how can you work like this? Is it all right? Is there any problem? I said, "No, I don't have any problems. Do you?" You know, it was more curiosity. This was what I was confronted with with this. I never in my life had a scene, you know, an out and out scene. The basic reaction seemed to me to be more curiosity, like how we could do this, rather than, "You dirty so and so, what are you trying to do?" I didn't run into any of that.
So the only time you really had -- ran into any absolute restrictions was in films, is that right?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
But never any other time. That's great.
No. Except later at the Palladium. Of course we never played there, because they had a -- they wouldn't hire a band that was mixed.
You're talking about the Palladium in Hollywood.
Except they'd hire Harry James because --
Willy didn't show.

Well, Willy was passing and so was Juan, and they didn't show. And of course Joe Comfort played there and he didn't show either, you know. Joe played there with me. That was all right. Which was so ridiculous, you know.
(Laughter)
That's really amazing that the Hollywood Palladium is the only -- you never lost any jobs? I mean found out you could not be booked?

Well, I lost the Palladium, but I don't consider it a loss, because at that time there were so many other ballrooms in California that actually paid just as good or better money. I used to like the Casa Manana better
than anyplace to play in. It was such a warm room and good feeling bandstand to play on and the crowd was great.
And there was no problem, they didn't object to mixed personnel?

Oh, no. They had a bunch of swinging dancers there. I mean that's what they wanted to do. You know, it was great for a jazz band to play at. Whereas the Palladium, you had to play everything, you know. The Casa Manana I loved. And then of course Tommy had the Casino Gardens - - Dorsey. We played there. We played the Aragon before Welk ever saw the place. We used to play out at Horace Heidt's Trianon Ballroom, and we played a place downtown, the Avadon, but -- they didn't lose anything, except possibly the -- you know, saying that you were able to play the Palladium, which was kind of famous. But I later played it and without any problems. So I don't figure I lost anything.

But the time when you couldn't play it was when it was operated as a full time band place where the Palladium hired the bands. When you later played it didn't you say that you played for another promoter?

Oh, yeah. Sterling Way was the manager there. We played a private party in there and we had been playing -- well, I played the Palladium when it was a week's job, and then I also played it when it was five days, and then I played it when it got down to three, and I played it when

it got down to two. One of these times when we were down, I think it was to three days a week they were going, one other day there we played an engagement for City College of Los Angeles, and I had Stuff Smith there and Joe Comfort in the band, and I went up to Sterling Way and I said, "Well," I said, "here we are. Stuff Smith's here and Joe Comfort's here and there isn't anything you can do about it, baby." And he said, "Well, it isn't me anyway. It's the policy of the owners."
And the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce, probably.
Who knows, you know.

Which used to be a terrible restrictive element in Hollywood. But when you finally did play it was when you were working with the Palladium management you couldn't play with a mixed band. Is that right?
No, they made it very clear that I wasn't welcome if I was going to have a mixed band.
So you just didn't tell them about Joe Comfort.
Well that particular time I wasn't working for them. I was working for City College of Los Angeles.
Oh, I thought you said that -- you told me earlier in the evening that you had already taken Joe Comfort in there.
Well, Joe Comfort had been in there. He'd been in there with me. He'd been in there with Harry James. He'd been in there with many bands. So that wasn't any big deal.
They just didn't know.
They didn't know, or it wasn't obvious enough to them that they cared to make an issue out of it.
I see.
But they didn't want anybody coming in featuring Roy Eldridge and -- or Peanuts Holland or Cat Anderson or somebody like that, you know, somebody that was quite obvious.
They're all right so long as they don't show.
Yeah, that's right.
How about Barney Kessel? When did he work with you?

Oh, Barney, I first got mixed up with Barney out here in Hollywood. He went to Hawaii with us right after the war in '46, and he played -- we did dates around up and down the coast here and everything. He was in the band.
Tell me about playing the Apollo. You're listed as the first[white] [inaudible] to play the Apollo theater in New York.
Well, that's true, unless you want to go back to the days when it was Hertig and Seamon's Burlesque
House and there was a white band in the pit then. But at that time the audience was mostly white.
How far back does that go?

Oh, that goes back into the '20s. But it's quite an old theater. It's been there for many, many years. Our first outing there at the Apollo was in 1934, and it came about more or less in an accidental way. Fletcher Henderson had broken up his band and Benny Carter had signed a contract to appear at the Apollo and he thought he was going to get -- believe it or not, there was a shortage, when I say competent black musicians, I mean guys that could read, you know. There was a lot of guys around that could play, but to play in a big band there was always a problem in those days to find guys that were capable of handling written arrangements in the discipline, you know, of a big band. And he was going to take the old Fletcher Henderson Band in there. Well, something happened. Fletcher decided to continue for another week or something and Benny was without a band. So the Apollo was hung up and Benny recommended us to -- this was before Frank Shiffman.] Frank Shiffman seems to have been forever there, but this was another guy that had this, the theater at the time. And Benny sold him on the idea of us playing there. And now this was the Park Central band, and we went up there and we were opened. Red Norvo, I had Red Norvo in the band. This is part of the Park Central band. I had Red Norvo doing his

thing with the xylophones and oh, he broke it up too, he really did. Of course you know Red was quite a performer before he became strictly a jazz player. I mean he was quite a showman. Did you ever see him chop that xylophone up? Well, he used to hit the xylophone. The climax to the whole thing is all the notes in the xylophone are -- he had a bunch of loose ones there, and they're flying all over the stage. It was sort of a comedy type thing.
No, I never saw that.

Oh, he used to get these soft mallets and he'd start banging away on these pieces of the xylophone, and they'd fly off into space and, you know, it was -- he had done this act in vaudeville. So he had a little act there that he did, and the band went over real good. Ralph Cooper was the master of ceremonies. Pig Meat Markham was there doing his thing, and [Puerto Rico] on the amateur night, you know, shooting the gun off and coming out in the grass. skirt and grabbing to grab all the people that didn't make it. That was my first -- from then on we -- I must have played the Apollo -- I used to play the piano, oh, four times a year, and it became, you know, a steady and wonderful experience. And through that we were also able to -- we had a chain of theaters that we inherited all the other black theaters around, like the Howard in Washington and the Royal in Baltimore and the Paradise in Detroit and the Regal in Chicago. We had our own little
circuit of theaters that no other white band had.
Wow.

And it was quite an experience. And I still say that is the greatest audience I have ever played to in my life. Boy, when that curtain came flying up and everybody -- it was an exhilaration, and they used to pour it on you. We did as many as eight shows a day there. We at one time held the house record for business.
At the Apollo?
At the Apollo. In fact, I don't know if you know this or not, but I came within 200 votes of being elected honorary mayor of Harlem.
When was that?
Oh, back in the -- around the time of '39 or around the time of, "Cherokee." Billy -- Willy Bryant beat me out by about 214 votes.
Aw. Now, that's an accomplishment. It really is.
Things ain't what they used to be.
(Laughter)
How -- tell me about Lena Horne working with the band.
Well, Lena came to us under a distressed circumstances on our part, and strangely enough through the Apollo. We were playing a two day theater up in the Bronx

called the Casino Theater, and I had a -- I had Ford Leary and Bob Carroll and I had a girl singer, too. I can't remember what her name was. Anyway, they all came down with laryngitis. Not one of them could make a sound. And this was one of these theaters where the band was the whole show. We had to play, put on, you know, an hour, hour and ten minute show, and if you've got no vocalists there again we get back to what I was talking about earlier, the static idea of watching a band play without something else happening. You know, when people are sitting there they want to see something. So in a panic I said, "My goodness, we're going to have to get somebody up here that can do something." So I called Clarence Robinson at the Apollo, who was like a producer and the dance director, and I said, "Clarence, is there anybody around there that can get up here so they can do something?" And I wasn't thinking as much of a singer as maybe some kind of an act or something. And he says, "Well, I don't know. A girl just left here," and he said, "She went down to the theater to go to the movies. I'll see if I can find her." Well, Clarence went down the street and went into the movies and ran up and down the aisle and found Lena sitting in there, and he said, "Get your gown and get up to the Casino Theater right away." So Lena came in. I'd never met her before. I didn't know who she was or anything, but naturally she's a very beautiful lady. So we had a talkover rehearsal down underneath the

stage, and she went on, and this was -- believe it or not this was an Irish neighborhood in the Bronx, and they are inclined to be very chintzy about -- like the manager came back and he said, "I don't know what's going to happen here." I said, "Never mind." And she went on and broke it up. And then of course I asked her to stay and she did, and she was with us for, oh, I think about nine months after that.

Did you read in her book where she said that she was all packed and ready to go back home to wherever it was that she'd been living with her husband that she was no longer really with, but back home to give up show business? She had her bags all packed --
Yeah, yeah.
-- in the YMCA and she for some reason didn't leave that minute, and instead decided to go see a movie because she was so depressed, and that was when Clarence Robinson came for her.
Uh-huh. Things happen funny, huh?
Yeah. Timing was really right on that time. How about travelling with her? She tells the stories about how wonderful you and everybody in the band was, but what a trial it was being on the road.
Oh, it was terrible.
The way the people were to her, I mean the public.

Well, the main problem -- of course nobody could deny her once she performed, you know. She was great. She was an absolute gas. But the problems came like the housing problems, see. So we used to have a gag we'd pull. The manager of the band would come in, and he'd say, "That'll be so many doubles," and he'd say, "And we want a single room for our Cuban vocalist." And he'd reel off a bunch of Spanish sounding words, I'm sure, like, (Speaking in fake Spanish), like that, and she'd say, "Si." And, oh that was all right. That was fine. As long as she was Cuban. And we overcame some of the problems that way, but -- and then of course when we went into the deep south one time, we were down at the University of Alabama, I said, "Lena, I don't think you'd better make this trip because we've got to play some funny places, and I can't see you being --," so I said, "We'll pick you up in two weeks. You're still on salary, you know, don't worry about it." And of course I got to the University of Alabama and that Dean ate my butt out for not bringing her. I said, "Well, I hope you can understand. I can realize that probably here everything would have been fine. But you must realize, I mean, the places we have to play to get here and to leave here." And he was a very astute gentleman, and he said, "Well, I guess we'll just have to forego the pleasure of hearing Miss Horne."
You know, she told about how she would

Yeah, it was murder. Of course then when she left the band that was quite a story too. She was my singer, we went in the Paramount, and Dinah Shore was the headline act, and of course as the band singer in the Paramount you always played an opening number, and then your girl singer came on. Well, Lena came on and when she got through there was nothing left for Dinah. And Dinah got sick. She said, 'I'm going to be sick until that girl is removed from the bill.'
Ooh.

And I said, 'Well, you're not going to remove --,' Bob Whiteman came back and I said, 'You're not going to remove anybody. I mean --,' He said, 'Read the small print in the contract.' And it says down there that the theater has the right to remove anybody from the show that they think is not for the best interests of the show and so forth and so on, and to edit any material that might be being used and so forth, if it was detrimental. And I went to Lena, and I had a contract with her. I've still got the contract, an unbelievable contract, $125.00 a week. And I said, 'Lena, I can't tell you, all I can say is your contract with me is yours if you want it. I can't protect you.' I explained to her. And I said, 'They're not going to let you go on anymore.' And

at that time -- I don't know, John Hammond or Leonard Feather or somebody like that, they got her in Cafe Society or something, and I said, "I think -- don't worry about any contract you might have with me, because if I can't protect you I don't deserve to have you." And of course she went on. And she was getting -- you know, a lot of people were noticing her, and she certainly didn't belong being a band singer. She was too much.
Yeah, well, I guess Cafe Society really got her career as a single off to a good start.
Yeah. And Dinah Shore came back to work.
Of course. Of course.
Now, I don't know if that was Dinah. It could have been her manager, because let's put it this way, Lena was murdering her. She couldn't follow her, you know.
Well, who could follow Lena anytime, today even?
Yeah.
When did Trummy Young work in your band?

Oh, he was with me in '43, maybe early '44. That was my second time back at the Park Central, and I had a complete mixed band then. I had -- I had five black people in the band with me there. I mean there was no token one

or two. This was just the way it was. I had Dick Vance, I had Trummy, I had Al Killian, I had Howard McGee and -- let's see, I had -- this trumpet player, I can never think of his name. I had it once and -- some years ago, and then I lost it again. But you talk about a band being loud, you know, this air conditioning wasn't in in those days, and they used to open the windows, and this was in the summertime, and we got complaints all the way from 5th Avenue.
(Laughter)

Eddie Burt was in that band and Dodo Marmarosa and -- and the two bass players, Chubby and -- oh, there was Oscar there, too. It was quite an engagement. A far cry from the band that was in there in '34.
I guess so.
Yeah.
And how about Frances and Neal, when did they work for you? Frances Wayne and Neal Hefti?

Well, Frances worked for me in '43. She was in that band. But she was there -- she wasn't there at the Park Central. Virginia Maxie was there. Frances joined the band -- she was there when Ralph Burns was with the band. Oh, wait a minute. Ralph Burns was there. It wasn't Dodo, Dodo came a little later. Ralph was still in the band there. Because I had heard her with her brother's band, and Ralph had been playing in that, and I wound up with both of them. And then Woody Herman stole Ralph from me, and then he wound up

with Frances. I used to break bands up. I mean it got -- it was -- of course at that time, I mean, I had a reason. I told you about the draft board, you know. It was a very uneasy thing. But I think I got my kicks out of building bands.
You sure built some beauties.
Well, at times. Sometimes they didn't turn out too well. But some turned out better than others. Let's put it that way.
Did Frances ever record with you?
Yeah. She made, 'Old Black Magic,' with me.
Oh, of course. She was a beautiful singer, and person.
Yeah.
And how long did -- did Neal -- you said that Neal wrote for you then too, didn't you?

Well, Neal joined my band as a trumpet player at first, in 1942. And of course he started writing for me then, and he would up with Woody too. But then he was back off and on, different times, playing and arranging before he got into his own thing. And we remain to this day very dear friends. In fact I just spoke to him the day before yesterday.
He's back here?
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
I know Leonard said he was coming back, but I -- I wrote to him when Frances died and I haven't heard from him. I didn't know, wasn't sure he was back.
Yeah, he just bought a home in Toluca Lake.
Not the same one?
No. No. He's going to live there with his son. And I said, 'How are you doing, Neal?' He said, 'I've got ups and downs, but it's getting better.'
She was one of the most remarkable people I ever knew, I think. Very, very special lady.

Oh, she was very much a lady. She just didn't fit the -- I'm not putting the gal singers down with the bands, but she's the most ladylike singer I ever had in my life. Now, I'm not saying that Lena Horne wasn't a lady, because she was. But you know, Lena could read somebody off if they came on too strong. But not Frances. Frances would just recoil in horror and gasp, you know.
But I think she could still handle things in her very lovely way.
Yeah. She always took care of things.
Nothing was beyond her, but she was different. It was a real privilege to know Frances, I think. Buddy De Franco.
Well, Buddy came on that band -- I call
that, I had the Mafia on the band there.
(Laughter)

Jimmy Pupa was the guy I got first, the first trumpet player, and he'd played first trumpet with Krupa, so I got him. You know, we used to steal people in those days. And he says, 'Well, you've got to get Dodo Marmarosa on piano,' and I said, 'Okay, we'll get Dodo,' when the piano thing came open. Then we got Buddy De Franco on there. Well, that band -- we went in the Strand Theater in New York, and they were completely out of hand. It --
