We were -- I said Buddy De Franco, and you said you'd just gone into the Strand Theater.

Yeah. This band was completely out of hand. This was during the war and some of the people we had in the band were very unstable, to put it lightly. So much so that -- well, various events like tying the hands of the clock backstage in a know, deliberately messing up the rising pit, so that it would jam on the way down, by running over to the side as it started down, and it would jam. And all sorts of minor atrocities. So much so that the management of the Strand called the union and the union sent a guy down and -- a guy by the name of Al Brown, and he said, "Look --," he collected all the union cards and he said, "One more incident and that's it." And he -- the theater really couldn't get too mad, because we were doing great business. They had them lined up all the way to 8th Avenue, and -- but it was just out of hand. I couldn't control them.
(Laughter)

Oh, we had a thing that we did in a strobe light, where we had some trick instruments that were painted with this substance that glows in the dark with a strobe light. Well, they would smear it on their nose and on their cheeks and they'd look like clowns up there, and everybody is laughing, you know, and oh, it was quite a scene. In fact, during the time there Dave [Schooler] called me and we

had a deal, we were going to go overseas for the USO, and I said, "Dave," I said, "these guys can't pass --," I'd have to come by for a physical is what he said, and I said, "Dave, these guys can't pass the physical. They're all 4-F." And he said, "Oh, this is nothing. All they've got to do is be breathing."
(Laughter)

He said, "Start sending them over about three or four guys in between each show. So this was -- I said after the first show, after the second show, after the third show. He had about 12 guys there, and he called me up and he said, "Charlie, don't send anymore guys over. I have found three dangerous paranoiacs, three dope fiends," and he said, "I don't know what's wrong with the others. But you would never be -- I can understand you might replace a couple of men to make this trip, but forget it, not this many."
(Laughter)
But it was a good band.
It was a good band, yeah.
Yeah. Well, it depends on what your criteria are, right? Buddy De Franco was in that band.
Yes. Although Buddy was a very orderly person. He was not -- like Dodo and Jimmy, you know, they were -- anything could happen. And then along with a few other
people in there, like Ray [De Geer] and very explosive people. Anything could happen, but no, Buddy was always very much of a gentleman.
How long did he work in the band?
Well, he worked up until that time when I disbanded that band on account of the draft board situation.
When did Fran Warren sing sign with you?

Fran came later. I think it was around -- oh, '46, around there. We played the Aquarium in New York, and I actually remember interviewing her at the Strand Theater. I believe -- I believe she replaced Kay Starr, if I'm not mistaken.
And Kay sang with you what, then, in '46, or '45?

Or '45, in there in that vicinity. And then Fran, you know, went with the band. We went on the road. She went out to California, up through Canada, and then we were back in New York at the Aquarium, and I always thought Frannie was one of the best singers I ever heard. She of course went into the musical shows and things like that, but if you could have kept her singing -- she used to want to sing too high, the keys, and I used to keep her down, you know, in a lower key, and I thought she sounded much better there, because where she wanted to sing and where she wound up singing -- oh, she did a wonderful job with Claude on "Sunday Kind of Love," but I always thought she was one of the best singers
around.
Uh-huh.

For a ballad. She couldn't do a rhythm tune, you know, but we didn't want -- we didn't need singers for that. We needed the singers for the ballads, because I liked to keep the tempo things for the instrumentals.
I read several accounts of your differences with [Beldon Cattleman] in Las Vegas, and I love the story. Tell it for me, will you?

Well, we were booked in there. This was a quintet. I had Buddy Childers and Ralph Pena Pinaud, Art Anton and Bob Harrington, and we were supposed to play in the lounge, you know. So the contract says 11:00 to 4:00, and we go up there, we play there a few days, and Beldon comes over to me and says, "We're changing the hours. You're going to play from 12:00 to 6:00." I said, "No, we're not going to change any hours." I said, "You're a businessman and I'm sure you read the contract before you signed it. I did." I said, "We're going to play 11:00 till 4:00." And he said no. I said oh, yeah. So the first thing he started, we'd go to work at 11:00 o'clock, and he turned off all the lights in the room and the mike, and we're playing up there all by ourselves, and we'd play, "Dancing in the Dark," and we'd start out in C and everybody would take a whole bunch of choruses on that, and then we'd go to D-flat and everybody'd -- the same tune --
and we'd play choruses on that, and we went the whole scale, you know. And then at 12:00 o'clock we'd turn the lights on. But then we'd quit at 4:00.
What did you play then, 'I'm Beginning to See the Light?'
No, we didn't play anything.
I mean at 12:00 o'clock.

Oh, no, he'd turn the lights on and then we'd just go ahead and do our thing, and he'd get up to dance, because they were able to dance there at the -- and every time he'd get up on the floor to dance I'd play, 'Cottontail,' at a breakneck tempo, you know, and --
(Laughter)

So finally he said, 'Well, tomorrow night you guys are going to play in the parking lot.' And I said, 'The parking lot?' So I called up Petrillo and I explained to him what was going on, and he sent him a wire. He said, 'Special scale for bands playing in the parking lot. Side man, $1,500.00 a week. Leader, $5,000.' Well, that was the end of that.
(Laughter)
So I finally compromised with him and I said, 'We'll give you one more hour, we'll play from 11:00 to 5:00, but I'm not going to 6:00.' So we finished the thing out.
That was what year?
Oh, I think that was around '53.
Was it El Rancho Vegas, was that the --
The Rancho, yeah, the El Rancho.
I like that.

Well, you know, a lot of guys said to me, "Aren't you worried about them guys up in Vegas?" I said I wasn't worried a bit, because all them guys, as you called them, hated Beldon. And they were secretly slapping their thighs and having a wonderful time about the whole thing. In fact I had a couple of them said, "Hang in there, kid. It's great. It's funny."
(Laughter)
I think it's the only case I ever heard of anybody standing up to anybody in Las Vegas, I mean management.
Well, I tell you, if it had been elsewhere I wouldn't have done it, but -- I'd probably be walking with a limp now --
If you were walking.
Yeah.
Barry Ulanov says that -- names you (Interruption in recording) -- that Don Redman arranged for, and you say no?
I was not fortunate enough to have any
But you mentioned that you were friends.
Oh, yes, I knew him well and for a long period of time. A wonderful little guy. He did teach me one thing, though.
What's that?
The perfect band rehearsal setup.
Which is what?

Which is you form a square, you have the rhythm section on one side, you have the saxophone sections on one side, and you have the brass section, the trumpets and the trombones, in other words, rhythm, trumpets, trombones and the saxophone section, and the guy that's rehearsing the band is right in the center. Everybody can hear each other, exactly what they're playing, and above all, the guy that's rehearsing the band can hear every note that's being played. It's the perfect rehearsal. I used to use it quite a bit.
That's very interesting.
Not many people do that. In fact I don't know anybody that does these days.
I went to an Ed Shaughnessy rehearsal and wasn't quite as square. It was more like a sloppy circle, but it was that principle.
Yeah.
Only Ed wasn't in the center. He was sitting on a platform behind them, but --
Well, was he actually rehearsing the band or was the arranger?
He -- well, no, you're right, the arranger was.
Well, see, that's the guy that should be in the center, because he can hear everything that's going on. There are no hidden things, you know, no covered up --
That's the only time I've ever seen it done.
Yeah.
That's interesting. Nonie Bernardi was in your band.
Yes, for a short period of time.
He spent more time with --
Tommy Dorsey.
And Benny Goodman too --
Yeah.
-- for awhile, right? We were talking about Johnny Hodges.
What is there to say?
I was telling you that in Baron's book he says that you were among the students of Sidney Bechet on soprano and you said no, not really. If you were -- you
didn't know Bechet, but if you were influenced by anybody --
It would have been John.
That's soprano as well as alto?
Oh, yes, yes, definitely.
And you were also saying that somebody said you didn't appreciate Charlie Parker or something and you were saying that --

Well, no, the question -- I was asked the question, how do you rate Johnny Hodges and Charlie Parker, and I said, 'I appreciate everything that Charlie Parker does.' If you know anything about music or saxophone playing at all you have to realize that this man was a giant. However, for my own personal taste, I would rather listen to Johnny Hodges just play the melody and phrase it in his own way. He doesn't have to do anything else, and that would please me much more than all of the acrobatics that Charlie Parker or Sonny Stitt or John Coltrane or any of them, I mean, might go through. This was a one -- nobody ever caught Johnny Hodges. There's no school, no Johnny Hodges school of playing, there never will be, because nobody could ever capture what he did.
How about Johnny as a person?
Oh, he's a wonderful guy. He was just a beautiful man.
You think his sound expressed him?
It had to. It had to.
I think so too. Mary Ann McCall sang with your band, you said twice, right?

Yes. Yes, she was with me, oh, I think around '40-'41, and then she was back with the band later. It may have been more than twice she was with the band, but she made a lot of Bluebird records with me. She was on a whole bunch of those. And of course she also sang with Woody, Woody Herman, and she kind of bounced back and forth there for a while, between Woody and my band. But I think she made more records with me than -- I know she made more records with me than she did with Woody. A great gal.
Yeah. You had Turk Van Lake.

Oh, Turk? A guitar player. When Turk was working with me he hadn't gotten in much, into arranging. He was just strictly, you know, a guitarist. And he wasn't with me too long because Turk didn't want to leave New York. He -- like the old story about Peck Kelly, did you ever hear of him?
I'm not sure.

Well, he was a fabulous piano player that lived back in the '20s, and he lived in Houston, Texas, and people would come from all over the country. He was just a fabulous piano player. And the old story was yeah, but you can't get him to leave town. He had offers from Paul Whiteman, no, he wouldn't leave. He stayed. I had the good fortune of

hearing him play. It was just fantastic. Of course the old school of piano, the full stride, Art Tatum type things, and in other words, the piano player in that school of piano, they had to sound like a whole band. They played their own accompaniment and the band and the solos and everything, but he was absolutely fabulous, but he would not leave Houston, Texas. And that's Turk Van Lake. I mean he would not leave New York.
Eddie Berk, trombone.
Eddie Bert?
Is it Bert or Berk?

Bert, B-e-r-t. Well, he was in the band at the same time that Trummy Young was. And of course they had quite a contest, because Eddie Bert was a very aggressive soloist, and as you know, so was Trummy. And it was a lot of fun, spelling them off against each other.
I've got to tell you a story about Trummy Young.
Okay.

We were playing the Howard Theater in Washington, and it seems that Trummy's wife was after him. And I came off the stage -- while an act was on, and here's all of these policemen there. The guy said, "We're after Trummy Young." I said, "What for?" He said, "Well, his wife, desertion and all this." So the next number on the bill happened to be "Mood Indigo," which starts off with a trio

up at the microphone of Trummy Young and a trumpet player and a clarinet. So that's the way it started off. Now the stage is very dark and now the trumpet -- the spotlight goes back to the trumpet section for an open trumpet solo by, I think at that time -- I think it was probably -- that was still Peanuts. And I got the word to Trummy. I said, "These guys are here waiting." So he got the stagehand, and we hoisted Trummy up in the flies, on a rope, up in the flies there. Now, it comes back to the trio at the end of the thing, now here is Eddie Bert, and the clarinet, you know, up there playing the thing. Now, these guys were furious. They said, "What are you pulling?" I said, "I didn't pull anything. We've got over 2,500 people out there in the audience. What do you mean pull anything?" "Well, you did something." I said, "I didn't do a thing. You can't prove a thing. How could I do anything? I'm not a magician, I'm a musician." Well, now we've got Chubby Jackson's -- that was our closing day there, and we were going to Boston, the RKO Theater in Boston. So we got Chubby Jackson's bass case and we put Trummy in it, and he was taken down to the station in the bass case on the truck, you know, and they couldn't find him. Oh, they were furious. Now, we forgot one thing. The story should have had a nice ending, everybody got away, but these were United States Marshal/s, being the District of Columbia. So when we arrived

in Boston they had another set of them waiting there for us because it was a federal charge. And it took my attorney all he could do to keep me and Trummy out of jail, and I had to come up with some money for Trummy's wife and everything. But we got a big kick out of that, you can see.
(Laughter)
And Chubby got his bass out too, right?
Well, he said, 'I want my bass with me,' you know.
(Laughter)
Life on the road was just one big adventure.
Well, you can sum up life on the road at that time, or anytime, I guess, you stay tired, dirty and drunk.
(Laughter)

There was much too much booze. Of course there's another saying. I think this was attributed to Artie Shaw, and it might have a little truth to it. He said, 'Jazz was born in a whisky barrel, reared on marijuana and is currently expiring from heroin.'
Gee, I hope he's wrong.

Well, of course this was around the time, this was said, was when heroin was very prevalent amongst the experimenters and things like that. But he's right in a way. If you analyze it, all of the early bands, they were all

booazers. And then along came Pops and everybody, you know, said if that's what you've got to do to play like that, we'll do that. Then along came Charlie Parker and the same thing happened. If that's what you've got to do -- there's a bunch of sheep, you know, in life, and they figure that you have to do all the bad things along with the good things, in order to be like whoever they're trying to be. It's unfortunate, but that's the way it is.
You were telling me, I think it was at dinner -- I don't think we have this on the tape -- about that out of sight trumpet section. We didn't get that on the tape, did we?
No.
Tell me about that trumpet section.
Well, that was the --
Oh, that's right, we were talking about John Howell, and that's how it came up.

Yeah. The '49 band, the trumpet section was Johnny Howell, Ray Wetzel, Maynard Ferguson, Doc Severinsen and Ralph Ericson. And it was something to hear, that trumpet section. They all made a contribution. Like Ray Wetzel was the disciplinarian of the group. I mean he'd say do it like this. And they respected Ray, believe me. This included Maynard and they respected his generalship. Of course Maynard had his thing and Doc had his thing and Ralph had his thing,
and then Johnny had his thing, but they respected Ray, and Ray ran -- actually was the general. And they did some remarkable things. I know Harry James came into Bop City and heard them and --
That's right, that band played Bop City in June, 1949.
I don't know, it was somewhere in there.
Yeah, I was there.

And Harry told me, he said, 'I never heard a trumpet section like this in my life. It's unbelievable.' Of course you're crazy, really, in a way, to get a trumpet section like that, because you know you're not going to keep these guys. They're going to peel off into their own thing and you're going to be left with a bunch or arrangements that nobody can play.
But what an experience while it's happening.
Oh, it's just wonderful to have had them.
Who else was in that band?

Well, let's see. Tiny -- well, Cliff Leeman was there for a while, but then Tiny Kahn took over on the drums, a beautiful man, left us very prematurely. And Eddie Safranski was playing bass, and Carlos Vidal had the bongos and the conga, mostly conga. And Claude Williamson was the piano player. And we had, let's see, Obie Masingill, Dick Kenney -- the other couple of trombone players escape

me. Let's see, there was Lenny something playing the alto saxophone player. Dick Hayfer, tenor. Dave Matthews, tenor. No, Dick Hayfer took Dave Matthews place. Kurt Bloom was playing the other tenor, and Reuben Leon, who's now a union official in L.A. Everybody gets old, don't they? Well, that's about it. The trombones -- I can't remember the other two. Oh, Kenny Matlock was one of them, and -- but it was a real -- but I've got to tell you something about that band. As great as that trumpet section was and as startling as the band was, I wasn't too happy with that. That band got out of my control. It was doing things well, but it wasn't doing the things I wanted it to do. I was uncomfortable with the band, although I appreciated it and I was very proud to stand there every night. You'd have to be. It was -- but the band had gotten out of my control. I had arrangers writing for me that were great arrangers, but what they were writing wasn't what I really would -- I let the band run me for the first time. And that is why I broke it up in October of 1949. Now, this -- many of those guys have never heard this. I would never let them know that I felt that way about the band, because I see them now and they say, "Hey, do you remember? Wasn't that great?" And yeah, I say it was great, but they don't know the real reason I broke that band up. The real reason was that I was inwardly unhappy with it, because it wasn't doing what I wanted it to do. They were running me. I wasn't running it.
And, well, that was it. We knocked it off on my birthday, October 26, 1949.
And that's when you went into business with Carlos?
That's when I joined Carlos for about six months.
With the thought that you would never play anymore, or what?

Well, I don't know. I sort of withdrew to regroup, because I had -- this experience had shaken me up quite a bit, the very fact that I let something get away from me, to get out of control. Because I was always in control before. And I had to really figure out, you know, what I wanted to do, if anything. Of course things were changing in music drastically then. You were -- it was a question of how far you wanted to go, you know, with what was going on, or if you wanted to stick by your convictions and -- it was a very tough period for me. And I think that was probably -- oh, I've had other bands since that I was very proud of, like the last band, in '66-'67, I was very happy with that band. That band was playing what I wanted to play and they were playing it the way I wanted it played, and they had the guys there that I wanted in the band, and so that was fine. But I think I had a real dry period from '49 on, because from then on I was in and out. I never had a really organized band after that. Some of the bands were quite passable and very good, but they

didn't approach the cohesion and the organization and the -- well, they just weren't organized like the older bands had been, and I like the idea of a constant personnel. I don't like this idea of -- and of course, as the band business matured and got on and on -- you can say matured, or maybe it got -- went the other way, I'm not sure. The idea of a fixed personnel, it became ridiculous. You had a parade of people going through a band, I mean, -- all -- the arranger became to the point where he wasn't writing for individuals anymore, he was writing for a group of people that played exactly this way and no other way, and if you didn't play that way you were a misfit. And I was unhappy with this, because I always believed -- I thought the Ellington theory was the best way. Write for the guys, the individual. And it became impossible to have a white band where you could have a constant personnel. And you can't be writing for people that are not there. So this became a question of a mob scene, writing arrangements for a bunch of guys, you know, anybody that comes along, which makes it very indistinct. Any wide interpretation of anything would be out of line, because the background that was written for any solos denied this. And also, there was a tendency in all of the soloists, every time they got ahold of eight bars it was like the Third World War. In other words, they never -- I used to tell them, "Why don't you listen to what's going on behind you? Listen to the

background. Now play something in there that fits. Don't, the minute it says ad lib solo, don't start playing the Arbens book, just because you've got eight bars or sixteen bars to shine. Listen to what's going on around you and try to fit something beautiful into that." This was gone, this was all gone. And I find -- I take umbrage with the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Band with this. They're going along, they've got a beautiful arrangement going, and all of a sudden some guy will come in with a solo, I mean, and just destroy the whole damn mood. It's like he's got to play everything he ever knew in his life, I mean, in that one outing. Now, this to me is wrong. I think I better get off the soapbox here.
(Laughter)
That's all right,hey. That's what -- you know, this is for -- this is your forum.
Have we covered the period between '46 and '49? We haven't talked --

Well, that was a band that included Clarke Terry and Jimmy Nottingham and Doc Severinsen, Joe Graves, and let's see -- oh, Dick Shanahan. That was a rather interesting period. That was the band that we finished this "Song Is Born" thing, and I finally got with the band. We had already gotten Clarke from -- what's his name, Hudson's band in St. Louis. Charlie Shavers put me onto him. And Clarke was in the band. Then we got Jimmy Nottingham. I

stole Jimmy from Lionel Hampton. Nice business, isn't it, stealing. That's a terrible -- but we had open -- I finally got with the band up in Portland there, and there was a little guy by the name of Sam Amato that I knew up there, a local musician, also in the produce business, and he said, "Hey, I've got a guy here you've got to hear." Well, sitting in on the job, nine times out of ten it's a disaster, you know. But this night it happened to be raining, and the people were leaving early and I said, "All right, wait till the last set. Where's the guy?" And here's Doc. Very young looking, you know, and everything, and he got up to play, and wow. I said, "Go home and get your clothes." He said, "Well, look, I don't want to take anybody's job." I said, "You're not taking anybody's job." I said, "We just added a fifth trumpet."
Gee.

So Doc came on. He started off on fifth trumpet, and finally winded up playing first trumpet, which he should have been doing all along, but I couldn't -- the guy was -- Jimmy Campbell was playing first trumpet and his lip went bad, and that gave the opportunity to move Doc up. But that was quite a trumpet section, too, although it didn't have the precision of the '49 trumpet section. The precision in that trumpet section was just something that was startling. But it sure had good soloists, players and
everything, like Clarke.
Did Clarke have a set style -- not a set style, but I mean an identifiable style?
Oh, that's the way he sounds today, the same way.
That early.
Yeah.
Because I wasn't aware of him that early, and --
George Hudson's band he came out of, in St. Louis.
I know he's from St. Louis.
Territory Band.
How long did Clarke stay with you?

Oh, he was with me about a year then. Maybe longer than that. Clarke I count as one of my dearest and closest friends. We're in touch all the time. I hear from him from all over the world and we get on the phone every now and then and just talk.

He sends me postcards with -- whenever I see him he always says, 'Hi, Pat,' on his trumpet, you know, not speaking, but speaks through his horn. And so I get cards from all over the world with the bell of a trumpet and, 'Hi, Pat,' coming out of it.
Yeah.
That's the message.
Oh, he's very busy with those cards.

Oh, he's quite an artist. I -- one of the -- one set of drawings made an impression on me, I'll never forget, and I keep asking him, you know, 'Where are they?' Duke was rehearsing at [Lewisohn] Stadium, and this was 1958, and I was wandering around the stage, taking pictures of the band, and I walked -- this was only rehearsal, and I could do that -- walked back behind the trumpet section, looked over Clarke's shoulder, and Clarke was drawing everybody in the band, but the trumpet's eye view. It's the way Quentin Clinton Jackson looked from behind, spilling over the side of the seat.
Oh, Yeah.
The way Paul Gonsalves Gonzalez looked asleep in his chair, from the angle of in the trumpet section. Shorty Baker taking a solo at the microphone, from behind.
Yeah.
It was marvelous.
You ought to see some of the art work I've got on some of my old arrangements, the guys who have got nothing else to do but draw.
You mean there's a lot of guys with --
Oh, there was an amazing amount of them, that they would sit back there and draw all kinds of -- some of them very pornographic, but nevertheless, it was art work.

I know when Kirstin Howell called John from my house, John told her to tell whoever it was that played lead trumpet in "Chorus Line" in Los Angeles, that he sure did appreciate the art work that arrived in Chicago, because the first trumpet music for "Chorus Line" was completely covered with pornographic drawings.

You know, the way some of those arrangements were marked up, every guy that would get in the band would have his own way of marking what was going on, and it's remarkable sometimes that a guy could even find out what he was supposed to do, I mean if you called a substitute in for some reason. They must have sat down and cried, because maybe this has been through a half a dozen different trumpet players, and they've all marked it differently. The same thing, but they've got a different way of marking it. It's -- I've got some old arrangements home there -- we had a copyist by the name of Emil Charlap, and he was a real artist, and he would draw these things in color on all the parts, actual pictures. Very humorous always.
(Interruption)

Leonard Feather, in, "The Book of Jazz," devotes some space to white bandleaders who hired black musicians, and there were so very, very few of them in the '30s and early '40s, and of course he gives you credit for having a mixed band, and he mentions the very few others, Artie Shaw having Billie Holiday in the band and Benny Goodman

having Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton, and Flip Phillips working with Frankie Newton. Let's see -- at Kelly Stables. But -- and Roy Eldridge, long association with Gene Krupa's big band. But this was something pretty rare during that period. Is that right? I mean --
Oh, yeah, it was rare all right. Although it actually -- I didn't do it to be revolutionary. It just -- it occurred to me as a wonderful idea. I said, "Why hasn't somebody done this?"
The reason probably was pressure, wasn't it, or was it?

Well, you see, I had never had any pressure that way, because I had never tried to do it, and I never got any pressure back in '34 when I had Garnet Clark playing piano up there and Benny Carter sitting back in the trumpet section on certain nights. I never heard a word from the management about it. You see, I never ran into this, and somehow or other I tend to find some of these stories must be greatly exaggerated. Maybe -- maybe these curious people that I'm talking about were met with some kind of antagonism, and they succeeded in turning these people into being angry about it. But I keep saying that the biggest thing that I -- emotion that -- if you could call it an emotion -- with any of these people that you would figure could cause trouble, it was more curiosity than anything else.

Do you suppose that maybe your attitude had something to do with it, that you took it or accepted it as curiosity, and therefore it didn't go in the wrong direction, whereas someone else took it as hostility?

That's what I'm saying. That's what I'm saying, Pat. I mean I would take the time to stand there and talk with them about it. And I think maybe other people took it as a hostile question, and maybe brushed the guy off or woman or whoever it was involved. They could have brought it on themselves. Because I never really had any problem that way, ever.
That's great. Well, there's certainly a lot to --

Like I never got screwed out of any money from any of the guys in the outfit, or the Mafia or whatever you want to call it, I always got paid, whether it came in or not. The only ones that ever screwed me out of any money have been like the Chamber of Commerce and the holier than thou people.
Uh-huh. Okay. How long did you stay in business with Carlos? Did you say it was about eight months?

Oh, maybe six months. It's hard to -- I found it very boring, very boring and irritating, and Carlos was a one man operation. Carlos never needed a partner of any kind. I mean he was a dynamo of a man, I mean in handling

the people he handled, and I think he realized I needed some sort of a thing, you know, a cushion to land on, after what I had done, and he provided it. I'm sure he didn't need me. I was very happy, though. At the time being it was something to do, give me a chance to sit down and think things out.
Whom did you manage?

Oh, Peggy Lee. We had Mel Torme. We had Nat Cole. We had Nellie Lutcher. We had Rafael Mendez. We had -- oh, let's see, there's something I'm forgetting there. Oh, June Hutton. And Woody Herman. So, you know, it was an interesting stable. I mean they're all people that you could be proud to say, "I represent them."
So after you decided you didn't want to be a manager, then what?
Oh, I organized a band.
(Laughter)

For about the umpteenth time. I started out with a -- I started out with, I think it was about eight men. Let's see. Yeah. And we came down here to San Diego here, and we opened in a place that's no longer there. And Neal Hefti wrote all the charts and Frances Wayne was back singing with me. And we played a bunch of places around. We were here, we spent about six weeks here, and got the thing together, and then we were booked around. We played a whole bunch of one nighters in Arizona and New Mexico, and on up in

the great northwest. In the meantime I had forgotten that I had a return clause engagement with Bop City, and they were insisting on it. And I flipped. I turned -- I was screaming on the telephone and they said, 'Well, you can take your choice. You can bring the little band in or you can come in with the big band, but you're going to come in.' And I thought, well, I can't go in there with a little band, you know, I mean after that other band. So Ray Wetzel was still with me. He was in the trumpet section. And I recollected a lot of guys, Dick Hyfer and some of the other guys, and I started -- now, this is funny. We're booked as an eight piece band, you know, and by the time we got up -- we were up in northern California someplace, I started to collect men for the big band, you know. I kept adding men. And this guy got on the phone to MCA and he said, 'What are you doing? I signed a contract for eight men.' He said, 'Barnet just walked in with 18 men.'
(Laughter)

And Hal Howard, was booking it, said, 'Don't worry about it. He's doing something. This isn't going to cost you anything.' But this guy was aghast, you know. He said, 'My God.' I said, 'Don't worry. This is not going to cost you anything,' because I was getting this band together. And as I found guys -- I knew I didn't have time to go through the process, you know, of building a band and keep working. I had to keep adding them and then as I found them, and we

came up with a pretty fair band. Johnny Markham playing drums and a good tenor saxophone player from up north whose name escapes me. And Ray was there and it was his generalship in the trumpet section, and he took some of the guys that were there and got them together pretty good. Al Porsino joined the band. And by the time we got to New York it was a pretty respectable band. And we went in and played Bop City and that's when I pulled my thing. I got in a bind with a wife of mine, and on top of that I had a boy singer by the name of Bill Derry, who was a great singer in the Eckstine vein band. He was a white man, but he had a great deep voice and he did all of Billie's tunes, and he did them well. And there was another singer on the bill. I can't even remember this clown's name, if you want to know. He used to sing out of the side of his mouth. I don't know if that brings back -- he had gotten one hit record or something. Anyway, his manager - - Bill Derry was killing him, you know, and his manager pulled this,he said, "Does Bill Derry belong to the union?" I said, "What union?" He said, "Well, he may be a singer with the band, but if he works in New York he's got to belong to --," AFTRA or something. Well, the result was they were going to pull Bill from the show because he was hurting this other guy, you know. He was a better singer than he was. So I don't know, I was drinking and I flipped, and I walked out, we started to play the opening number and I absolutely flipped. I walked out in the middle of the stage in Bop City

and I stopped the band. I said, "I've been wanting to do this all my life. You can all go fuck yourselves." And I took my soprano and I broke it over my knee and walked out of the club, downstairs, and got in a taxicab and went to the airport and took a plane to California. Now, that is exactly what happened.
Wow. Did the band finish the engagement?

They kept the band. The band was playing, and then five days later, the hardest thing I ever had to do in my life. I walked in there and -- oh they were -- now they're scared, these hoods that had that joint, you know. They said, "Will he sue us? Will he sue us?" They figured I'd had a nervous breakdown, which I guess I did in a way, but it wasn't serious, you know, it was just a flipola. But they were scared I was going to sue them. Because I had fought them. I didn't want to play the place, you know, and they knew that. And they figured that they had caused this upheaval. So the hardest thing I ever had to do in my life, Pat, was like five days later I got on the plane and walked back there, and I walked in right before the show and I walked backstage like nothing has happened and just took over where I left off. Never said a word to the band. The band never said a word to me, and we finished the engagement. And these guys never said a word to me.
How wild.
(Laughter)
Good for you. So --

In the meantime, I had a valet who had been with me for like 18 years, Curry Wilson, what a doll. He had gone out and he had gotten the horn repaired. He got it all straightened out and everything, all the keys put back on, because it was a mess. I really -- it was bow-shaped, and I had a big bruise on my knee. They're pretty hard, you know, those sopranos.
But you felt better. This is really going back, but you felt better after you did it, didn't you?
I don't know. It had to happen. It had to happen. Something had to happen. Something awful had to happen. I'm glad it was that way, I didn't hurt somebody or something, you know.
Just you, your leg.
Yeah.
So from Bop City, that would be 19 -- what, about mid-'50?
Yeah.
Yeah.
Where did you go from there?
Well, I went back -- let's see, I went back to the little band and I was working around. The big bands were starting to die then, you know. It was very -- I

played around some terrible joints. I had to step over a dead body in one joint to get out the back door. I mean I didn't know he was dead at the time. I thought he was drunk and asleep. I found out the next day he'd been shot there. And I finally wound up in -- it was out here. I worked out in California with the big band, doing some dates around locally, playing weekends and things like that. And then I went back to the little band after that. And after a couple of scenes, like I said, stepping over this guy, and some of the -- the first time I ever ran into problems about getting paid, you know, and I said this is not for me. I joined Martha Raye, down at the Five O'Clock Club in Miami Beach, in '53, early '53, and I was there all summer with her. It was a small band, but it was a lot of fun. I mean every night was New Years Eve, and it was a delightful experience, because she's a wonderful gal. And she went to Vegas out of there, and she asked me to go along, because her music was so screwed up. Most of the parts were missing, and everything was -- it was a case of like I was telling you about, musicians marking everything, and she wanted me to go to Vegas to rehearse the band and explain to them what happened with the music, because she couldn't explain it, with all the markings and everything there, which I did. And after I got her straightened out there was no place for me there. I didn't belong to the Vegas local, and I had a situation there where her husband thought I was making time with Martha, and it was a bad scene, you know, which

I wasn't you know, but he was very jealous and drunk all the time, and he thought something was going on, and what was going on was she'd had it with him and he was looking to blame anybody he could blame. So I got out of that scene. And I had this little band I put together, with Buddy Childress, like I told you. We came back and we played the El Rancho and some other places, and we went up to Alaska. We were up there for two weeks, up in Anchorage. And if I'd have stayed up there another week I think I'd have come home in a box, because we went up there to entertain -- we were playing on the base, the Elmendorf Air Force Base, and they figured that they had to entertain us. So like very night, it was just terrible. I was a physical wreck when I got home from there. Then I played around some more clubs around L.A., and we went to -- back to Florida. We played the Dream Lounge with this band there, Buddy Childress again, and then we went over in the Bahamas. We played over there, in Nassau. Then we came back and we played Palm Beach, at a place there. And oh, that was -- it was society belles. Something else. One of them dragged me out at intermission, got me out on the beach, and she wanted to -- like, "Let's make it right now, baby." I said, "You've got to be kidding." She said, "No. My husband is drunk. Why don't you come over to the house later and we'll --," I said, "Hold the phone. None of that stuff, you know." So we came home from there, and let's see, Arnold Ross

was in that band and Paul Sarmento and Buddy Childress, and Boone Stines was the drummer, a guy out of Oklahoma, a guy that had a good beat but no technique. And then I -- this guy at MCA, Bob Wooling, said, "Look, you shouldn't be fooling around with this gig. Why don't you play the Palladium." I said, "They won't let me in with a mixed band." He said, "You don't have a mixed band. You don't have any band. What are you talking about?"
(Laughter)

So I started -- I put a band together there with a bunch of guys out here. There were a bunch of good guys out here then. There was, you know, Porfido, and Maini Charlie Kennedy and Joe Maney and -- a whole bunch of guys, guys that had been with me and other guys, and we rehearsed, and we played the Palladium and we played a season over in Catalina, and we'd play -- we were doing very nicely here, just playing weekends around L.A. And we never went -- and I would make a trip a year back east. I would go back -- I'm talking about the '50s now. I would go back, maybe I'd take one or two guys with me or -- Nat Pierce was back there then, and he would contract, he'd get a bunch of guys together, and well, I played Basin Street a couple of times, one time before the band I was talking about before. And we would then go out on the road and play the south and up in New England and up to Canada and, oh, about a six week one nighter tour, and then I'd come back to California and leave the band there, bring

the couple of guys I'd brought with me, if any, and it was working out, except for one thing. You're doing nothing but maybe making a living and nothing constructive or creative, and I started to lose, frankly, to lose interest. And I'd do these things because it was a matter of money, and of course when my mother died -- I did that right up till '63, when my mother passed away. I came into quite a bit of money. And I didn't have to do anything, and I didn't do anything until about '66. Well, in '66 I started -- she passed away in '63. For three years I just didn't do anything, musically. Well, I had a lot of things -- problems about settling the estate and other things. Well, anyway in '66 I got the itch again, and it looked like there was a little resurgence for big bands. Buddy Rich had come in this place and made a big hit, and I went into the place and we bombed.
What place was that?
That place on Santa Monica, the --
The Chez?

Yeah, horrible. An awful joint. But the only reason I went in there at all was Basin Street wanted me back with the big band, and I wanted to go to New York one more time, and Clarke and I had a pact, and Nat Pierce, and we had talked about it. I said, "If I can get Basin Street we're going to do this and we'll do that." It

was all agreed. So I called them and I said, 'All right, I've got the deal set. Are you guys still ready to go?' 'Yeah.' So I wanted a place to reacclimate myself to being in front of a band, and The Chez presented that, the feeling of leading a band, and also the mechanics of it. Because you forget, you get away from it, you know, I had to learn my own arrangements over again, plus put a lot of new ones in, which I did. And we played there two weeks, and business was not good. But I took Willie Smith with me. That's the only guy I took from California. And the other guys were waiting in New York. Clarke and Nat have gotten all these guys together and we rehearsed and we opened, and the band -- it was a gasser. Like the union had a beef about something there, and the guy came in and heard the band -- Vincent Battali or something like that -- he said, 'Oh, I couldn't do anything to hurt this band.' He said -- and they actually figured out a way to circumvent their own law so they couldn't disturb the band, which I thought was very singular, because 802 is notoriously the hell with you.
Right.

But we were there four weeks, and we were the only ones in the show that got paid. The Four Aces were on there -- not the -- the Four Tops. They were on there. They got stiffed. And there was another gal in there that was one of the -- the outfit put her in there. She was a very

nice little girl but she didn't belong in this company, you know, but I presume -- whether she got paid or not was unimportant. It was the exposure they wanted. But they didn't get paid. But this guy that had that place, I went to him. I said, "Look, are you going to pay me?" I said, "I hear rumors of how the joint's going to fold after New Years." And business, we were doing good business there, but the joint hadn't been doing good business. And he looked at me and he said, "You'll get paid." And by God, I did. And I'm the only one. And Joe Glazer had handled the Four Tops, and they didn't get paid. I did.
Gee.

So that was when the man with the moving picture came in, and we did that and oh, we wound up, we made a whole bunch of transcriptions for the Navy, and we did the Tonight Show, and I was running around --
The whole band?
Yeah, sure.
Did the Tonight Show?
Yeah.
Wow, what happened with the Tonight Show band?
Well, they weren't --Clarke was working for me. He wasn't in -- he was working in my band. He wasn't working the Tonight Show band the whole time.
Yeah, but did they just dismiss the Tonight Show band to bring your band in, or were there two bands on the show?
Oh, yeah, the Tonight Show band was there until they brought us on, and we finished out the -- they've done that a few times. They did it with Harry James.
I didn't remember their having a whole other band on, just parts of a band.
Well, see, the way that's done is they don't pay for that.
Oh.

It's usually paid for by a record company, and in my case I wanted to do it so mine was paid for by Indigo Music Incorporated, a music publishing firm which I owned. And this is what happens anytime -- a lot of times the groups that go on there, they're not paid by NBC. This is the biggest racket in the world. They get away with murder. They use every angle in the world to keep the overhead down, and they're making millions off of that program. But it was all right with me. I figured gee, things are going good. This is probably my last fling. Let's go out in style, you know, let's do the Tonight Show. So we set it up and it didn't cost much. What the heck, the scale wasn't too much, and we'd done all these other things, and the pot was -- I wasn't in it to make any money anyway. I was having a ball, a good time.

So actually, Pat, that was -- oh then I had an engagement in Las Vegas after that, which I'd already signed, and there again I was going to take Willy up, but I was going to put together a Las Vegas band. Unfortunately, Willy passed away.
So Willy's last work was with you.
Yeah.
And the last time he would have been on film was that film made in New York.
Right. That's right.
And the last recordings would have been those transcriptions you made, right?

The transcriptions, the sound track, and also the album we made in Hollywood before we went east. They were all with me. I did the Las Vegas thing, and well, that was that. As far as I'm concerned that was the end of me in the band business. I've done a few other things since then. I put a band together and played Disneyland, and -- it was a hell of a band. Of course I spent more money on the band than I got because I rehearsed for five days to play two nights, and paid the guys for rehearsal, because I wanted it to be good.
When was that, what year?
Oh, that was, I think, '72. And it was good. Even Leonard Feather liked it.
Well, then.

He said we blew Basie and everybody, Lionel Hampton, right out of the park, or words to -- different words than that, but -- anyway, Cat was in that band, and a lot of other guys, a lot of good players. And the only other thing I've done since then is I went up to Canada in '73, and -- I think I've previously mentioned that, fronting the CBC Orchestra for a week. And that's it. That closes the lid as far as I'm concerned.
You don't want to play anymore.
No. No. I'm very definite about that, Pat. What I want to do I can't do and if I can't do what I believe in and what I want to do, then I'm not going to do it.
No, I don't blame you . What do you mean, you can't do?

Well, I don't think physically I could take the road. When I say physically, mentally. I don't think I could take static from people and the arguing that goes along about what you're going to play and what you're not going to play, from people. I don't think I -- I think my fuse is too short.
Well, you shouldn't have to take it, at any time.
I mean I wouldn't take any crap from anybody now, you know what I mean? And you get a lot of crap in front of the band, from people.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

You were telling me between tapes --

Oh, we were talking about -- I said there's a whole bunch of stories, you could call them human interest stories, but some of them are pretty high comedy. One in particular, got into town in Youngstown, Ohio, and when you're on the road, of course a lot of times you don't exactly have female companionship, so I checked into the hotel, and I was driving my own car and the band was in the bus, and I got down to the hotel, and I said, "Where is the best whorehouse in town?" And the bellhop told me where to go, and I got in a cab and I went out there, and as I drove up, here's a great big Greyhound bus out in front of it with an electric sign on it that says, "Charlie Barnet and His Orchestra," and the whole gang is inside there, they had taken over the joint.
Knowing the value of publicity, they got you billing in there too.

Oh, beautiful publicity. But it was -- so many outrageous things happened, I mean that it's really more a life story, than shall we say that has to do with the music world, although it did happen on account of the music world. But I want to get back to one thing, and that was that I said that '73, that appearance up in Canada was the last thing I've done, and probably will be the last thing I've done

musically, because I've turned down, oh, feelers from -- Willard Alexander calls me every once in a while and says, "Hey, what about --," I know exactly what happened, he found one big money date and he wants to hinge a whole tour on one date, and then you've got to go through all that, the arrangements I have are getting old. I would have to get some new things, and I would have to buy a wardrobe. My whole lifestyle has changed, and I'm very happy with it. I'm into a different thing, fortunately, because I was able to do it gradually. I didn't just cut it off and say that's it, and I started changing over, and I am into a different lifestyle and I like it.
You spend, you said, seven months of the year, is that right, in Palm Springs, in the desert --
And five months here. And if we feel like taking a trip someplace we take it.
That's wonderful.

And it's -- I'm very happy with it, and I cannot under any circumstances ever imagine myself going back in the band business, although I do enjoy hearing a good band, and when they come around where they're near me and I can go hear them, I do.
So long as you don't have to come into Los Angeles, right?
Well, I don't have anything against Los Angeles, except that I have no base of operations there anymore.

I've got the place here in San Diego and the boat, and I've got my home in Palm Springs and this is just fine, because we get the same bands here in San Diego that appear in Los Angeles, and they're a lot more accessible here. Like Stan Kenton has been here, and Woody Herman, Harry James, Count Basie. They had Count Basie playing out at the ballpark here one year. He played for three days, before the game. And in between innings. And I sat right down there, with the band in front of me, and it was just wonderful. And there was a big crowd. He was set up right off of third base, and he had more people around him than were watching the game, because the Padres are not exactly a thrilling ball club at this point. And Stan was here, I went over to see him, the same place that Woody played, and Woody, the whole band was flying from San Diego to Baltimore on a plane. This kind of operation -- both of them told me the same thing. They said, 'We never made more money in our life, but it goes in one pocket and out the other.' The expenses are just colossal.
Well, the expense of transporting a band.
Oh, sure, and everything else connected with it. And I think I mentioned -- I don't know if I mentioned it on the tape or not, about Woody? We were talking abnd --
That wasn't on the tape, no.
It wasn't on the tape? He was over at the table and I looked up at the bandstand and I said, 'Woody,

do you remember when we were stealing men from each other back in the '40s?" I said, "None of these guys were even born then." He says, "You're right." It's -- and Stan's the same, he's up there with a bunch of real young guys. He gets them -- they both get them out of the same source, North Texas State and Indiana and the Berklee School of Music and back in Massachusetts. And these guys come out and I don't know where they're going to go, because only a fraction of them can make it into the studios. There's only so much room there. What happens to them? Because they're not -- there's a band at -- back in Illinois. What is it, Henniken, or -- Milliken. Milliken University. The director of that band knew me some years ago and he wrote me a letter and asked for some arrangements, and I sent them to him, and he sent me, for the last three years -- they make a record, an LP, every year. And this band is just great. It's a better band than any band that's on tour today, with one exception, the soloists. They all come out plastic. They're all out of the same mould. There isn't any individuality. But ensemble, the band is as good as any band that's touring anyplace. Now, there's a lot of colleges, a lot of places like that, and there's a lot of these guys that are very proficient. They read like a hawk. They execute. But like I say, they're plastic. But if the band business ever were to come back, which it never will as we knew it. It's completely out
of the question. A lot of people keep saying, 'Oh, when is it coming back?' Well, it's not coming back.
Willard says it is.
Huh?
Willard says it is. Of course that's his business. Willard Alexander.
All right, where's his new bands?
He says that --
Maynard Ferguson and his 13 angry men?
(Laughter)
He said every band that he's handling has got a full itinerary, months ahead, and there's lots and lots of work.

Well, true, but who is he handling? He's handling ghost bands, the Glenn Miller Band, the Jimmy Dorsey Band, the Tommy Dorsey Band. Well, he's got Kenton and he's got Maynard Ferguson and Woody Herman. But where are the new bands, Pat? Where are they? There aren't any new bands. And this is the whole thing. I mean it's almost impossible today for a new band to get started. You could say Buddy Rich is a new band if you want to. But Buddy Rich is not a new band. Buddy Rich is an old name which a band was built around. But there are no youth people. Maynard Ferguson's an old name. He played with me, he played with Kenton. This is not new. And when you show me where there's a new band that's really

making it, or bands, let's put it that way, then you might say there might be a resurgence in the band business. Although I can't see economically where they could possibly make it. Even in our time there were angels. Maria Kramer at the Lincoln-Edison Hotel. She -- well, we were involved in a deal. She was involved with Jan Savitt. She was involved with Gray Gordon, with Blue Baron, owned a piece of the band in return for putting them in there and putting us in there, you know, for the air time, and she got a cut off the top until the union stopped it. You had A. Edward Masters, the attorney. He had two bands that he had financial investments in. Johnny Long and Jerry Wald. And they had investments up to $50,000.00 at that time, and neither one of them really got off the ground. Do you imagine what it would cost today to get a band off the ground, with the way -- like when you used to have an arranger on salary, you know, like $75.00 a week or something, or a hundred and a half if he was a real good arranger, for all he could turn out in that time. Today it'd cost you three or four times that just to get the arrangement copied, not to mention the guy that makes the arrangement. And then if you want to use it in a night club, that's fine, but if you want to record it you've got to pay them and the copyist all over again. If you want to make it in a movie you've got to pay the copyist and the arranger all over again. If you're going to play it on television you've got to pay the arranger and the copyist all over again. You wind up with over $2,000.00 an

arrangement. There's no way in the world that a new band can overcome those costs. That's why I say there will never be the big band business. Now when we -- God forbid -- when we lose the guys that are still out on the road, the names of anybody that is left there, there won't be any names left, and then where is your big band business? Willard is trading on what happened before. He's not trading on anything new. Period. I rest my case.
Okay. Well, when Willard comes back into town in a week or two he told me he's going to bring me all kinds of evidence, because we were talking about doing a story, but I've got to see.

Well, I'm sure this is correct. I mean there is -- there are enough people that want the big bands, but you know what they want? The want Glenn Miller. They want to hear Glenn Miller tunes. They want to hear the Tommy Dorsey hits. They don't want to hear anything new, these people.
Yeah.

I've run up against them. I got on a disc jockey program over in Palm Springs. It was billed -- a discotheque for big band lovers. I almost got into a fist fight with the guy. And when I stormed -- I walked off the program, because these people didn't -- they wanted -- this was everybody that ever knew anything about a band. They were the "Melancholy Baby," people and the -- they don't want anybody doing anything new with a big band. They want to hear the old
Glenn Miller things, the Tommy Dorsey hits, the Benny Goodman hits. They want to hear "Cherokee," but they don't want to hear anything new.
Yeah.

So it's a -- this is all wishful -- I can understand Willard. After all, as you said, this is his business. And Willard is getting up there, too. And how many champions are there for the big band business? After Willard who is there?
Right, hardly anybody. Nobody cares. That's not where the money seems to be. You've got to really be devoted to work for a big band at this point.
Fortunately we've got Woody, you know, and Basie, and the ones, you know, the other guys around that are still left. But that's not going to go on forever.
Right. Is it true what Leonard reported in the "Book of Jazz," that you were once publicized as the White Duke?
Yeah. Yeah.
Whose idea was that?
It wasn't anybody's idea that I know of. Somebody -- I don't know who was responsible for it. It certainly wasn't Leonard.
No, he was just reporting it.
But I believe it was probably somebody

that reviewed a show someplace, maybe a Variety -- it sounds like something one of the Variety reviewers might have written, when they review a stage show or something. Because we used to do a lot of the stage mechanics like the Ellington band did. We operated back of a scrim and we had production numbers and things, like Duke used to do. And it was possibly -- I would say it must have been a Variety review that sponsored that thing.
And it sort of hung on for awhile?
Well, anytime you put a label on something, other people pick it up and who knows.

I presume that you are familiar with Clarke Terry's account of his joining your band, the first time he played a solo? It was in Stanley Dance's book, the interview with Clarke Terry. Do you know -- do you remember this? Clarke says, 'Charlie Barnet called me from California while I was working the Riviera, a big plush sort of place where Ellington swears he originally wrote, 'Sophisticated Lady.' I didn't know a soul in Charlie's band and the only person I knew in L.A. was Gerald Wilson. He took me over to where the band was playing and I walked up to the bandstand. The band was on the air and Charlie motioned me to go around the back and onto the stand. The next thing he was announcing, 'Now we'll hear from our new trumpet player, Clarke Terry, who has just arrived'. It was one of his originals, 'Charleston Alley,'

or something like that, and it wasn't too difficult, but it was a big chance to take, on the air, coast to coast. Ellington does things like that too. I stayed with the band for one of the happiest years of my life, until Charlie got lonesome for his swimming pools, private plane and yacht. Charlie's the most wonderful person in the world."

I have to come back and say Clarke is the most wonderful person in the world. I think something like that did happen. But I used to enjoy putting people on the spot like that, particularly when I knew they were perfectly capable of handling it.
But the story really did remind me of -- it's the kind of thing Duke would do. And usually a person who's very capable, even if they're terrified, will come through, because of that pressure.
Oh, sure.
But did you know how good Clarke was, really?

I hadn't heard him play, but I had complete faith in Charlie Shavers, and I mean, I talked a great deal -- when you go and send for a guy from St. Louis -- I had talked very long with Charlie about Clarke, and after what he said and as much faith as I had in Charlie, I had no qualms about it at all.
A little earlier we were talking about
Billy Strayhorn, and I don't think we've talked about him on the tape.
Uh-huh.
What do you particularly remember about Billy Strayhorn?
Well, let's see. "Prelude to a Kiss," "Warm Valley," "Chelsea Bridge," "Passion Flower," and a lot of other beautiful things.
You were telling me that during your long friendship with Strayhorn you repeatedly asked him for just eight bars?

Oh, yeah. I kept saying to him, you know, I said, "How about writing me an arrangement?" And he would say, "No, I really can't." And I would say, "Well, look, just eight bars. How about eight bars and we'll build a whole thing on it," and I never did get the eight bars. But we used to joke about it. It became a thing. He was a fantastic man. He -- I can't think of any greater complement to Duke than his finding Billy Strayhorn, because it was such a wonderful mixture. Billy Strayhorn gave a delicacy to the Ellington band and a warmth that even exceeded Duke's efforts in those areas. And I've often wondered, as we were talking about him, between tapes, I mean, how he felt about some of the things that were credited to Duke which were really his work. But apparently it didn't bother him, and of course he

couldn't have found anybody to interpret what he was doing -- well, you get back to the old thing, the alter ego, the association there. You couldn't tell where one left off and the other started, and without each other -- well, let's put it this way. I doubt very much if we'd have heard much about Billy if he hadn't gotten associated with Duke, because he was too subtle in a very rough world of music. Of course I think if I could have found him I might have been able to do something, but on the other hand where would he have gotten the soloists? I never had the soloists that Duke had. Well, you keep bouncing back and forth. I mean if one, what would the other had done, and the other and the other and the other. It comes back that I think that was truly an alter ego situation.

Yeah. They had an amazing kind of a communication, and were, as you say, great complements, because Duke needed the attention and Billy didn't care about it, which was fine, because if they had both wanted recognition there would have been a clash.
Oh, it would have been a catastrophe.
But Billy was content --

They'd have been in court, arguing about who wrote this eight bars and that eight bars. Because I know of a lot of cases where they actually did, one would start an arrangement and the other would finish it.
Uh-huh.

It's a question of where -- who owns it the, you know? But Billy did write a lot of things that were either erroneously credited to Duke or -- I won't go so far as to say deliberately, but I mean Duke Ellington was so big that anything that came out of there automatically -- even if Juan Tizol did it -- it was credited to Duke, because it came out of there. He was such an awe inspiring figure.
Uh-huh. But the difference with Billy was that Billy didn't care.
No, Billy didn't care.
So long as the music got written and --
Barney was a little salty about it.
Yes, yes, Barney was, and still is a little bit, although he's philosophical. He -- I don't think he's mad at anybody, but he said there was 20 years of royalties he could have used.
Yeah. Pat, it's getting cold.
Oh.
Damp, I think is the word.
And late?
Yeah, it is.

In Valerie Wilmer's book, (Interruption in recording,) -- she says Babs Gonzalez's first name job was with Charlie Barnet in 1944. "He toured with alto saxophonist's big band for several weeks, but never recorded, mainly because

You say this was in 1944?
That's what it says in the book.

Well, that's strange because Lena Horne was with me in '40 and '41, and was long gone in '44, and while I've known his nibs Mr. Gonzalez for a long time he never worked for me. He's a very amusing guy, and he never toured with the band. To my knowledge he was never on my payroll for anything.
Okay. We took care of correcting that one.
A guy that did work for me for a long period of time was Bunny Briggs.
Oh.

One of the -- oh, the greatest dancer. We used to -- I had him on practically every Apollo show and other places. I had him where he couldn't even dance, he would just sing. We had numbers that he sang, and he had such a wonderful personality, I mean he broke up everyplace that we went into with Bunny. Bunny unfortunately had a big mother complex. he was completely dominated by her and I think he could have been a big star if it wasn't on account of this. Fortunately, I had the pleasure of having him with my band on many, many occasions. He was just an absolute blockbuster as far as breaking up a show.
Oh, he's a great dancer. I know I've heard him sing, too. But I didn't realize he'd worked with you. What year was it?
Oh, I found Bunny dancing on a tabletop in Baltimore back in, oh, about 1941, something like that. And he was with my band, oh, up till 1950.
Steadily or on --

Practically steadily. As steady as the band happened. I mean he was there. He was down in Birdland when it was known as The Clique. He was there with me. I had him with the '49 band. I had him in numerous -- every theater I ever played I made sure he was on the bill with me, including the Paramount and the -- in New York, and all of the other theaters around the country. I'm talking about the white theaters, too. I'm not only talking about the black theaters. And I also had him with the band, and occasionally where he couldn't dance, all he did was sing. And exhibited his personality. He's with Lionel Hampton now.
Oh. I didn't know that.
He does a lot of work with Lionel now.
I didn't know what he was doing now. I knew he worked with Duke briefly.
Yeah.
In the first Sacred Concert and some other dates.

Yeah. But he'd get away from home, he'd get homesick. He'd want to go home, you know. I said, "Buddy --," I had him out at Universal Pictures. They put him in one of these shorts as an audition. They were very interested. He says, "No, I've got to go home." I said, "Bunny, you don't know. You're on the verge of something here." "No, I've got to go home." It was really sad.
That is a shame.
